Beyond Quadratic Attention

The complete book of the project: what we built, why, how, what we found, and everything that went wrong along the way

Written for TheOneAboveALL, and for anyone who wants to understand this project from zero.

Every number in this book was measured on this machine during the project. The raw data lives in experiments/results/ and the generated reports live in experiments/reports/. Wherever a number appears, the run it came from is named so that you can open the file and check it yourself.

How to read this book

This book assumes no prior knowledge. It begins with what a vector is and ends with the details of how a fused attention kernel moves memory through a CPU cache. If you already know a topic, skip ahead; every chapter starts with a short "what you will learn" box and ends with a "key points to remember" box.

There are three kinds of text:

  • Explanations, which teach an idea from first principles.
  • "In the code" boxes, which point to the exact file and function that implements the idea, so you can open it and read along. File paths are relative to the project folder C:\Users\omjee\OneDrive\Desktop\PROJECTS\Beyond Quadratic Attention.
  • "What actually happened" boxes, which tell the true story of the project: the mistakes, wrong turns, bugs and how each was found and fixed. These matter. Real research is mostly finding out why something does not behave as expected, and this project had many such moments. Chapter 22 collects all of them in one place.

Chapter 1 — The whole project in one chapter

What you will learn: what the project is for, the one question it asks, what was built, what was measured, the most important findings, and the shape of the rest of the book.

1.1 The problem in plain words

Modern AI language systems such as chatbots are built from a design called the Transformer. Its key ingredient is an operation called attention: every word (more precisely, every token) in a piece of text looks at every other token and decides how much to "pay attention" to it.

"Every token looks at every other token" is the problem. If a text has 1,000 tokens, there are 1,000 × 1,000 = one million token pairs. With 10,000 tokens there are 100 million pairs, a hundred times more work for only ten times more text. Mathematicians call this growth quadratic: double the length and the work quadruples. That is why long documents are expensive for AI systems, and why researchers have invented many cleverer ways to compute attention.

This project is a laboratory for studying those ways. Not a single program that does one thing, but a collection of tools to implement, verify, measure and compare different attention algorithms on an ordinary laptop.

1.2 The one question

The project brief stated the central question like this:

How do attention algorithms trade off computational complexity, memory traffic, numerical accuracy, and practical execution speed as sequence length increases?

Each phrase in that sentence turned into a part of the project:

Phrase What we built to study it
"computational complexity" an analytical model that counts operations and memory for each algorithm (Chapter 12)
"memory traffic" memory instruments that measure how many bytes each algorithm actually allocates (Chapter 13)
"numerical accuracy" a correctness laboratory comparing every method with a high-precision reference (Chapter 11)
"practical execution speed" a benchmarking system with careful timing and background-load monitoring (Chapter 13)
"as sequence length increases" sweeps over lengths from 64 to 16,384 tokens (Chapters 14–15)

A second question came from the fact that some algorithms do not compute exactly the same thing as standard attention. They approximate or restrict it. For those, we also asked: what do you lose? That led to the quality experiments (Chapters 16 and 18).

1.3 What was built

Everything lives in one folder and runs locally. Nothing is sent to the internet.

Eight attention implementations (Chapters 7–10):

Name Family One-line description
naive exact the textbook formula, written plainly; the "ground truth" everything else is compared with
sdpa_math exact PyTorch's built-in attention, forced to use its plain "math" path
sdpa_flash_cpu exact PyTorch's built-in attention, forced to use its fused, tiled C++ kernel for CPUs
tiled exact our own implementation of the online softmax / tiling idea behind FlashAttention, written in Python
tiled_recompute exact the same, plus a custom backward pass that recomputes instead of storing; this is the trick that saves training memory
local_window restricted each token may only look at nearby tokens
block_sparse restricted tokens are grouped into blocks, and each block may look only at selected blocks
linear_elu different function "linear attention", which replaces the exponential in softmax with a simpler formula that can be reorganized to avoid the quadratic cost

Tools around them:

  • a numerical-correctness laboratory: 795 comparisons of every exact method against the reference, in three number formats, with an explicit and justified tolerance policy;
  • a complexity model: formulas for operations and memory per method, checked against counters built into the algorithms;
  • a benchmarking system: repeated timing with statistics, three different memory instruments, a memory guard that refuses to run configurations that would exhaust RAM, isolated worker processes, and a monitor that records how busy other programs kept the CPU;
  • controlled tasks: hand-built "retrieval probes" and small Transformer models trained on synthetic tasks, to measure what the approximate methods lose;
  • a command-line interface (python lab.py ...), a local web interface (Streamlit), automatic reports with tables and figures, and a test suite of more than 400 tests.

1.4 The machine

The brief described an AMD Ryzen 5 5300U. The actual machine, checked on day one, has an AMD Ryzen 5 7530U: 6 cores, 12 hardware threads, AVX2 vector instructions, a 16 MB L3 cache, 16 GB of RAM, Windows 11, Python 3.13.3 and PyTorch 2.10 (CPU build). There is no NVIDIA graphics card, so every result in this book is a CPU result. GPUs behave differently, and Chapter 13 explains how.

A fact that shaped the whole project: the computer was shared. Throughout the work, other programs from other projects kept between 5 and all 12 logical CPUs busy, and free memory was often under 1 GB. The project had to learn to measure honestly under those conditions (Chapters 13 and 22).

1.5 The most important findings

Each of these is explained in detail later, with its evidence.

  1. All exact methods compute the same function. In 64-bit floating point they agree with the reference to about 10⁻¹⁵. In 32-bit, every method passed every forward and gradient check (Chapter 14).
  2. How you store intermediate numbers matters more than the algorithm. Computing attention entirely in the 16-bit bfloat16 format gave errors up to 38 %, while the kernels that keep intermediate values in 32-bit stayed at 0.3 % (Chapter 11).
  3. Tiling removes the quadratic memory, but not the quadratic time. At 2,048 tokens the reference allocates 194 MiB per call, while the tiled and fused methods allocate under 5 MiB. Yet every exact method's time still grows like length squared (fitted exponents 1.9–2.1) (Chapter 14).
  4. Tiling alone does not fix training memory. Letting PyTorch's automatic differentiation run through the tiled loop brings the quadratic memory back (exponent 1.72). A custom "recompute" backward pass keeps it linear, and was also faster: 0.98 s against 1.85 s for the autograd version at 2,048 tokens (Chapter 14).
  5. The same algorithm can be 3× faster or slower depending on how it is executed. PyTorch's fused C++ kernel and our Python tiled code implement the same mathematics, but the fused one is about 3× faster (Chapter 14).
  6. Approximate methods are faster only beyond a crossover length, about 2,048 tokens for local-window and block-sparse attention on this machine. Below it they are slower than the fused exact kernel (Chapter 15).
  7. Surprise: the approximate methods used more memory than the fused exact kernel, 16–27× more at 4,096 tokens, because they store their restricted score tables while the fused kernel stores almost nothing (Chapter 15).
  8. Restriction has predictable costs and sometimes benefits. Local attention cannot retrieve anything beyond its window (accuracy drops from 100 % to 0 % exactly at the window edge). Yet on a task needing only local information, it generalized to 4× longer texts better than full attention (100 % vs 87 %) (Chapters 16 and 18).
  9. A model that "learned" a task may have learned a shortcut. Twice in this project a model appeared to solve a retrieval task but had found a shortcut: once in the data generator, once through fixed positions. Finding those shortcuts is told in Chapter 19.

1.6 How the work proceeded

Roughly in this order (the true, messy history is in Chapter 22):

  1. Audit: inspect the empty folder, the hardware and the installed software.
  2. Reference implementation and its tests.
  3. Tiled exact attention (online softmax), then the recompute backward.
  4. Numerical validation across shapes, masks, magnitudes and number formats.
  5. Approximate methods.
  6. Benchmarking system and complexity model.
  7. Experiments: correctness, memory scaling, timing (repeated after the background-load problem was discovered), approximate-method scaling, tile sizes, threads, shapes and dtypes.
  8. Quality: probes, then trained models, then the long MQAR investigation.
  9. Interface, reports and documentation, followed by a final audit.

Key points to remember

  • The project is a laboratory for comparing attention algorithms on speed, memory, accuracy and quality.
  • Eight implementations: five exact, two restricted, one different-function.
  • Everything was measured on a shared, CPU-only laptop, and the project measures and reports that load.
  • The headline: memory efficiency, speed and accuracy are different things. An algorithm can win one and lose another, and the winner depends on length, threads and hardware.

Chapter 2 — The mathematics you need, from zero

What you will learn: numbers in lists (vectors) and tables (matrices); the dot product; matrix multiplication; exponentials and logarithms; the softmax function; what a gradient is and why training needs it; and "big-O" notation for describing how cost grows. Everything else in the book builds on these ideas.

2.1 Vectors: lists of numbers

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, for example [2, -1, 0.5]. The number of entries is its dimension; this one has dimension 3. In AI, a vector is how we represent a thing: a word, an image patch, a position. Each entry captures some aspect of it, though usually no single entry has an obvious human meaning.

In this project, each token is represented by vectors of dimension d (we mostly used d = 64).

2.2 The dot product: how similar are two vectors?

The dot product of two vectors of the same dimension multiplies matching entries and adds the results:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [4, 0, -1]
a · b = 1×4 + 2×0 + 3×(−1) = 4 + 0 − 3 = 1

Why it matters: when two vectors "point in the same direction" their dot product is large and positive. When they point in opposite directions it is large and negative. When they are unrelated it is near zero. Attention uses the dot product to measure how relevant one token is to another.

Computing one dot product of dimension d costs d multiplications and d − 1 additions. In this book one "multiply-add" counts as 2 floating-point operations (FLOPs), so a dot product costs about 2d FLOPs.

2.3 Matrices and matrix multiplication

A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers with rows and columns. A matrix with L rows and d columns is called "L × d". You can think of it as L vectors stacked on top of each other, one per row.

Matrix multiplication C = A × B (requires A to be m × k and B to be k × n) produces an m × n matrix where each entry C[i][j] is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B:

A (2×3) = [[1, 2, 3],        B (3×2) = [[1, 0],
           [0, 1, 0]]                   [0, 1],
                                        [1, 1]]

C = A × B (2×2):
C[0][0] = 1·1 + 2·0 + 3·1 = 4      C[0][1] = 1·0 + 2·1 + 3·1 = 5
C[1][0] = 0·1 + 1·0 + 0·1 = 0      C[1][1] = 0·0 + 1·1 + 0·1 = 1

Cost: m × n dot products of length k, so about 2·m·n·k FLOPs. This formula is used throughout the book.

The transpose of a matrix, written Bᵀ, swaps rows and columns: an L × d matrix becomes d × L. If Q and K are both L × d, then Q × Kᵀ is L × L, and entry [i][j] is the dot product of row i of Q with row j of K. That single matrix product computes the similarity of every token with every other token, and its L × L shape is where the "quadratic" in this project's title comes from.

Tensors

A tensor is the generalization to any number of dimensions: a vector is a 1-D tensor, a matrix is 2-D, and so on. Attention in this project uses 4-D tensors shaped [B, H, L, d]:

  • B: batch, how many independent texts are processed together;
  • H: heads, how many independent attention computations run side by side (Chapter 4);
  • L: length, how many tokens per text;
  • d: head dimension, the length of each token's vector.

2.4 Exponentials and logarithms

The exponential exp(x) = eˣ (with e ≈ 2.71828) turns any number into a positive number: exp(0) = 1, exp(1) ≈ 2.718, exp(−1) ≈ 0.368, exp(10) ≈ 22,026, exp(−10) ≈ 0.0000454. Two properties matter here:

  1. It is always positive, which makes it useful for building weights.
  2. It grows explosively. A difference of 10 in the input is a factor of about 22,000 in the output. That is exactly what lets attention focus sharply on one item. It is also what causes overflow: exp(89) is already too large for a 32-bit float (Chapter 3).

A key identity: exp(a − b) = exp(a) / exp(b). Online softmax (Chapter 8) is built on it.

The logarithm log(x) is the inverse: log(exp(x)) = x. The quantity log(Σ exp(xᵢ)) is called log-sum-exp (LSE). It appears in Chapter 8 as the single number per row that the memory-efficient backward pass stores.

2.5 Softmax: turning scores into weights

Given a list of scores x₁, …, xₙ, the softmax turns them into weights that are positive and sum to 1:

softmax(x)ᵢ = exp(xᵢ) / (exp(x₁) + exp(x₂) + … + exp(xₙ))

Worked example, scores [2, 1, 0]:

exp(2) ≈ 7.389,  exp(1) ≈ 2.718,  exp(0) = 1        total ≈ 11.107
weights ≈ [7.389/11.107, 2.718/11.107, 1/11.107] ≈ [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]

The largest score gets most of the weight, but not all of it: softmax is a "soft" version of picking the maximum. Scale the scores up and it becomes harder: [20, 10, 0] gives about [0.99995, 0.00005, 0].

The shift trick. Adding the same number c to every score does not change the softmax, because exp(xᵢ + c) = exp(xᵢ)·exp(c) and the exp(c) cancels between top and bottom. Programs therefore subtract the maximum score before exponentiating, so the largest exponent is exp(0) = 1 and nothing overflows. This is called the stable softmax, and every implementation in the project uses it (Chapters 7 and 8).

2.6 Weighted averages

If weights w₁ … wₙ are non-negative and sum to 1, then w₁·v₁ + … + wₙ·vₙ is a weighted average (also called a convex combination) of the vectors vᵢ. Attention's output for each token is exactly this: a weighted average of "value" vectors, with softmax weights. A consequence used in Chapter 11 is that an attention output can never be larger than the largest value it averages.

2.7 Probability and a few statistics

  • A probability distribution over n outcomes is n non-negative numbers summing to 1, which is exactly what softmax produces.
  • Uniform guessing among n options is right with probability 1/n. For example, chance level for 16 possible answers is 6.25 %. That number appears in Chapter 19.
  • The median of repeated measurements is the middle value after sorting. It is robust to a few extreme values, which is why our timing reports use it (Chapter 13).
  • The inter-quartile range (IQR) is the spread between the 25th and 75th percentiles, a robust measure of variability.
  • Cross-entropy loss measures how much probability a model gave to the correct answer: loss = −log(p_correct). If a model spreads probability evenly over n answers, p_correct = 1/n and loss = log(n). So a training loss stuck at log(4) ≈ 1.386 means "uniform over 4 options", a fact that was crucial in the MQAR investigation (Chapter 19).

2.8 Derivatives and gradients: how learning works

A derivative says how much a function's output changes when its input changes a little. If f(x) = x², its derivative is 2x: at x = 3, nudging x by 0.001 changes f by about 0.006.

For a function of many inputs, the list of derivatives with respect to each input is the gradient. A neural network is a big function with millions of adjustable numbers (parameters). Training repeatedly does three things:

  1. compute the loss (how wrong the network is);
  2. compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter. This step is called the backward pass, or backpropagation, while computing the output is the forward pass;
  3. nudge every parameter a little in the direction that reduces the loss (an optimizer such as AdamW decides exactly how).

Two things to remember for this project:

  • The backward pass usually needs values computed during the forward pass. Keeping those values in memory is what makes training use much more memory than inference (just computing outputs). This is central to Chapter 8.
  • The chain rule combines derivatives of nested functions. PyTorch's autograd applies it automatically: it records every operation in the forward pass, then replays them backward. Writing a custom backward means doing this by hand, which tiled_recompute does.

2.9 Big-O notation: how cost grows

"Big-O" describes how a cost grows as the input gets larger, ignoring constant factors:

Notation Name Doubling the input multiplies the cost by
O(L) linear 2
O(L log L) "n log n" a bit more than 2
O(L²) quadratic 4
O(L³) cubic 8

Standard attention costs O(L²·d) time: the L × L table of dot products, each costing O(d).

Measuring the exponent. If time t grows like L^p, then log t = p·log L + constant, so a plot of log t against log L is a straight line with slope p. The project fits that slope to measured data (reporting/report.py::fit_exponent). A fitted exponent near 2 means "quadratic in the measured range", and near 1 means "linear". This is how theory and measurement are connected in Chapters 14 and 15.

Big-O hides constants, and constants decide real speed. An O(L) method that does 100 operations per token loses to an O(L²) method doing 0.01 operations per pair until L > 10,000. Chapter 15 measures such a "crossover" on this machine.

Key points to remember

  • Dot product = similarity. Q × Kᵀ = all pairwise similarities = an L × L table.
  • Matrix multiply cost: 2·m·n·k FLOPs.
  • Softmax turns scores into positive weights summing to 1, and it is unchanged by subtracting the max.
  • Attention output = weighted average of value vectors.
  • Loss stuck at log(n) = uniform guessing among n options.
  • Training needs the backward pass, which needs stored forward values, which needs memory.
  • Fitted log-log slope ≈ growth exponent: 2 = quadratic, 1 = linear.

Chapter 3 — How computers store and compute numbers

What you will learn: bytes and memory sizes; the memory hierarchy (registers, caches, RAM) and why moving data often costs more than computing with it; floating-point numbers and rounding; the three number formats used in the project (fp64, fp32, bf16); CPU cores, threads and parallelism; and what Python, PyTorch, tensors and autograd are.

3.1 Bytes and sizes

A byte is 8 bits. Memory sizes in this book use binary units: 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes, 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes (about one million), 1 GiB ≈ one billion bytes. "MB" and "GB" are used loosely for the same ideas.

A 32-bit floating-point number (fp32) occupies 4 bytes. So an attention score table for one head with L = 1024 tokens holds 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 numbers, which is 4 MiB. With 4 heads that is 16 MiB. At L = 4096 it is 64 MiB per head and 256 MiB for 4 heads. Keep these sizes in mind; they explain most of Chapter 14.

3.2 The memory hierarchy: why moving data is expensive

A CPU does arithmetic on numbers held in tiny storage slots called registers. Data must be brought there from main memory (RAM), which is large but slow, through a series of caches, which are progressively smaller and faster:

Level Size on this machine Rough speed
Registers a few KB per core instant
L1 cache 32 KB data per core (384 KB total) ~1 ns
L2 cache 512 KB per core (3 MB total) a few ns
L3 cache 16 MB shared ~10 ns
RAM 16 GB ~100 ns and limited bandwidth

(The sizes were measured on this machine with Windows' Win32_CacheMemory; the speeds are typical orders of magnitude, not measurements.)

The crucial consequence: an operation that does little arithmetic per byte is limited by how fast data can be moved, not by how fast the CPU computes. This is called being memory-bandwidth-bound. Adding up a large table, or applying exp to every entry, is memory-bound. Multiplying two large matrices is compute-bound, because each number fetched is reused many times.

Naive attention creates L × L tables and makes several passes over them (scale, mask, subtract max, exp, sum, divide). Once a table exceeds the 16 MB L3 cache (at L = 1024 with 4 heads), every pass goes to RAM. Much of the speed of an optimized attention kernel comes from never writing that table to RAM at all (Chapter 9).

3.3 Floating-point numbers

Computers store real numbers in floating-point format, a binary version of scientific notation: value = sign × mantissa × 2^exponent. The mantissa (significant digits) has a fixed number of bits, so most real numbers can only be stored approximately: they are rounded to the nearest representable value.

The size of the rounding is described by the unit roundoff u: the relative error of a single rounding is at most about u.

Format Bits Mantissa bits Unit roundoff u Largest value Used here for
fp64 ("double") 64 52 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁶ ~10³⁰⁸ the reference ("ground truth")
fp32 ("float") 32 23 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ ~3.4 × 10³⁸ default for all benchmarks
bf16 ("bfloat16") 16 7 3.9 × 10⁻³ ~3.4 × 10³⁸ low-precision experiments
fp16 ("half") 16 10 4.9 × 10⁻⁴ 65,504 tolerance defined, not benchmarked

Three consequences matter in this project:

  1. Overflow. exp(x) exceeds fp32's maximum when x > 88.7, and becomes inf (infinity). Then inf / inf = NaN ("not a number"). The stable softmax (Chapter 2) prevents this.
  2. Absolute precision shrinks as numbers grow. bf16 has only 8 significant bits, so near 256 the gap between neighbouring representable numbers is about 1. A logit of 300.4 might be stored as 300. For softmax that is a disaster: an error of 0.5 in a logit multiplies its weight by e^0.5 ≈ 1.65. This is the cause of the biggest numerical finding in the project (Chapter 11).
  3. Addition is not associative. (a + b) + c can differ from a + (b + c) in the last bits. Two correct programs that sum in different orders therefore give slightly different answers. That is why we compare with tolerances, not exact equality (Chapter 11).

Special values: inf and -inf (overflow, or deliberately used for masking: exp(-inf) = 0), and NaN, which poisons every computation it touches.

3.4 CPU cores, threads and parallelism

A core is an independent processor. This machine has 6 physical cores. Each can run 2 hardware threads (simultaneous multithreading, SMT), giving 12 logical CPUs, but two threads on one core share its arithmetic units, so they rarely give 2× the speed.

PyTorch splits large operations across intra-op threads using a library called OpenMP: a matrix multiply might be divided into 6 pieces computed at the same time. Coordination costs time (starting the pieces, waiting for the slowest one, a barrier). For large operations the overhead is negligible. For tiny operations it can exceed the useful work. If another program is using a core, the piece running there is delayed and every other thread waits at the barrier. Chapter 15 shows this happening: the Python tiled code became 4.8× slower with 6 threads.

torch.set_num_threads(n) sets the thread count in our code. The environment variables OMP_NUM_THREADS and MKL_NUM_THREADS set it before PyTorch starts.

Vector instructions (SIMD). A single CPU instruction can operate on several numbers at once. This CPU supports AVX2 (256-bit registers: 8 fp32 numbers per instruction) but not AVX-512, and it has no native bf16 arithmetic. That is why bf16 is not faster than fp32 here (Chapter 15).

3.5 Python, C++ and the cost of "dispatch"

Python is the language this project is written in. It is easy to read but slow at doing many small things, because every line is interpreted. C++ is compiled to machine code and is fast.

PyTorch is a Python library whose heavy work is done in C++ (and specialized libraries: MKL and oneDNN for matrix math on Intel/AMD CPUs). When Python calls a PyTorch operation such as a @ b, PyTorch must:

  1. parse the arguments and check types, shapes and devices;
  2. choose the right C++ implementation (the dispatcher);
  3. allocate memory for the result;
  4. record the operation for autograd, if gradients are needed;
  5. run the C++ code.

Steps 1–4 cost a few microseconds, regardless of how big the operation is. For one huge matrix multiply that is negligible. For 10,000 tiny ones it is 10–50 milliseconds of pure overhead. This dispatch overhead explains why our Python tiled attention, which issues roughly 10 small operations per tile, is slower than the C++ fused kernel that implements the same algorithm (Chapters 8, 14 and 15).

3.6 Tensors, autograd and memory in PyTorch

A PyTorch tensor is an n-dimensional array with a data type (torch.float32, …) and a device (here always the CPU). Some operations return views, which reuse the same memory with a different shape (for example transpose, expand, unfold). Others allocate new memory. The project relies on views to avoid building large masks (Chapter 7).

Autograd: if a tensor has requires_grad=True, PyTorch records every operation applied to it in a graph and keeps the intermediate tensors the backward pass will need. loss.backward() walks the graph backward and fills each parameter's .grad. The kept intermediates are why training memory is larger than inference memory, and why "letting autograd differentiate through a tiled loop" keeps all the tiles alive (Chapter 8).

torch.inference_mode() and torch.no_grad() switch recording off. Our forward-only benchmarks use inference mode, so they measure the computation without autograd bookkeeping.

The CPU allocator. PyTorch requests memory for each new tensor from its CPU allocator. The profiler can record every allocation and free, with sizes and timestamps. The project replays those events to measure the peak memory of a call (Chapter 13).

Key points to remember

  • One fp32 number = 4 bytes. One L × L fp32 table at L = 1024 = 4 MiB; with 4 heads = 16 MiB = the whole L3 cache.
  • Moving data is often the real cost, so avoiding large intermediate tables is the main lever for speed.
  • Floating point rounds. u is fp64 1e-16, fp32 6e-8, bf16 4e-3. exp overflows fp32 above 88.7.
  • bf16's coarse spacing at large magnitudes ruins softmax logits unless they are kept in fp32.
  • Python dispatch costs microseconds per operation, so many tiny ops are slow.
  • More threads help large operations and hurt tiny ones, especially on a busy machine.
  • Autograd keeps forward intermediates alive for backward: that is training memory.

Chapter 4 — Transformers and attention, from scratch

What you will learn: what tokens and embeddings are; what a Transformer is made of; exactly how attention computes its output, worked through by hand with real numbers; why the scores are divided by √d; multiple heads; masks (causal, padding, custom); and how a model knows where each token is (positional encodings, including RoPE, which this project uses).

4.1 From text to vectors: tokens and embeddings

A language model cannot read letters directly. Text is first cut into tokens (words or word pieces), and each token is replaced by an integer ID from a fixed vocabulary. In this project the synthetic tasks use a vocabulary of 64 IDs (Chapter 17), for example "ID 9 = a key symbol" and "ID 25 = a value symbol".

Each ID is then turned into a vector by an embedding table: a learned matrix with one row per vocabulary entry. Token ID 9 becomes row 9, a vector of d_model numbers (64 in our models). A sequence of L tokens becomes an L × d_model matrix.

4.2 The Transformer in one picture

A (decoder-only) Transformer is a stack of identical blocks. Each block has two parts, each wrapped in a "residual connection" (the input is added back to the output) and preceded by a LayerNorm, which rescales each token vector to a standard size:

x  →  x + Attention(LayerNorm(x))      ← tokens exchange information
   →  x + MLP(LayerNorm(x))            ← each token is processed on its own

After the last block, a final LayerNorm and a linear "head" turn each token vector into scores over the vocabulary: the model's prediction. The MLP (multi-layer perceptron) is two matrix multiplies with a nonlinearity (GELU) between them. It processes each token independently. Attention is the only place where tokens interact. That is why attention gets all the attention, and why its cost dominates long texts.

In the code: src/attention_lab/models/transformer.py — TinyTransformer, Block, Attention. The Attention module computes Q, K and V, then calls whichever attention algorithm you choose by name. This "plug-in" design (Chapter 6) lets the same model run with any of the eight implementations.

4.3 Queries, keys and values

For each token, attention computes three vectors by multiplying its representation with three learned matrices:

  • Query (q): "what am I looking for?"
  • Key (k): "what do I contain?"
  • Value (v): "what will I hand over if you pick me?"

For a sequence, these form three matrices Q, K, V, each of shape L × d (one row per token). Then:

S = Q Kᵀ · (1/√d)          scores: how relevant is token j to token i?        (L × L)
P = softmax(S, per row)    attention weights: each row sums to 1                (L × L)
O = P V                    output: each token's weighted average of values      (L × d)

In one line, as in the original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al., 2017): Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d) V.

4.4 A worked example by hand

Three tokens, d = 2. (The numbers are invented for illustration, then checked with the project's own naive_attention.)

Q = [[1, 0],      K = [[2, 0],      V = [[1, 0],
     [0, 2],           [0, 1],           [0, 1],
     [1, 1]]           [1, 1]]           [5, 5]]

Step 1: scores S = Q Kᵀ. Entry [i][j] is query i dotted with key j:

token 0: q=[1,0]: with k0=[2,0] → 2;  with k1=[0,1] → 0;  with k2=[1,1] → 1
token 1: q=[0,2]: → 0, 2, 2
token 2: q=[1,1]: → 2, 1, 2

S = [[2, 0, 1],
     [0, 2, 2],
     [2, 1, 2]]

Step 2: scale by 1/√d = 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071:

[[1.4142, 0.0000, 0.7071],
 [0.0000, 1.4142, 1.4142],
 [1.4142, 0.7071, 1.4142]]

Step 3: softmax each row. Row 0: exp(1.4142) ≈ 4.113, exp(0) = 1, exp(0.7071) ≈ 2.028; total ≈ 7.141, so the weights are [0.576, 0.140, 0.284]. Doing all rows:

P = [[0.5760, 0.1400, 0.2840],
     [0.1084, 0.4458, 0.4458],
     [0.4011, 0.1978, 0.4011]]

Every row sums to 1. Token 0 pays most attention to token 0. Token 1 splits equally between tokens 1 and 2.

Step 4: output O = P V. Each output row is a weighted average of the rows of V:

token 0: 0.576·[1,0] + 0.140·[0,1] + 0.284·[5,5] = [1.996, 1.560]
token 1: = [2.337, 2.675]
token 2: = [2.407, 2.203]

The project's naive_attention returns [1.99595, 1.56001] for token 0, matching to rounding.

4.5 Why divide by √d?

If the entries of q and k are random with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product (a sum of d products) has variance d. With d = 64 the typical score would be about ±8, and the softmax would almost always put nearly all weight on one token. Its gradients would then be tiny, and learning would stall. Dividing by √d brings the variance back to 1 (Vaswani et al., 2017, footnote 4). The project's default is scale = d^(−1/2), and a test checks it (test_scale_is_one_over_sqrt_d).

4.6 Multiple heads

Instead of one attention with vectors of size d_model, the model splits the vectors into H heads of size d = d_model / H and runs H independent attentions in parallel. Each head can specialize: one may look at the previous token, another for matching content. The outputs are concatenated and mixed by a final linear layer. All of this is why our tensors are 4-D [B, H, L, d]: batch × heads × length × head-dimension.

4.7 Masks: forbidding some pairs

Often some query–key pairs must not interact. A mask removes them by setting their score to −∞ before the softmax, because exp(−∞) = 0 gives them zero weight.

  • Causal mask. A model that predicts the next token must not peek at future tokens: token i may attend only to j ≤ i. In the example above the causal weights become [[1, 0, 0], [0.196, 0.804, 0], [0.401, 0.198, 0.401]]: token 0 can only see itself, so its output is exactly v0 = [1, 0].
  • Padding mask. When texts of different lengths are batched together, short ones are padded with filler tokens that must be ignored. Our key_padding_mask has shape [B, L], with True meaning "real token".
  • Custom masks. Any boolean table (True = allowed) or an additive table of numbers (added to the scores, −∞ removes) can be supplied.

The project defines the semantics of all masks in one place (algorithms/base.py, class MaskSpec), matching PyTorch's own convention (Chapter 7).

Edge case: a fully-masked row. If every key is forbidden for some query, the softmax is 0/0, which is undefined. The project's policy is output zero and zero gradient, chosen after checking that this is what PyTorch's own CPU kernels do. The story is in Chapter 7.

4.8 Where am I? Positional information

Attention by itself ignores order: shuffle the tokens and each output is the same weighted average, just shuffled. Models therefore add positional information:

  • Sinusoidal absolute encodings add a fixed pattern of sines and cosines, different for each position, to the embeddings (Vaswani et al., 2017).
  • Rotary position embedding (RoPE) rotates each query and key vector by an angle proportional to its position (Su et al., 2021). The dot product of a rotated query at position i and a rotated key at position j then depends only on the difference i − j. The model therefore naturally sees relative positions. Our models use RoPE by default, and a test checks the relative-position property (test_rope_scores_depend_only_on_relative_position).

RoPE is applied before the attention algorithm is called, so every attention implementation receives the same Q and K. Keep RoPE's relative-position nature in mind: in Chapter 19 it is exactly what allowed a model to solve a supposedly content-based task with a purely positional trick.

4.9 Exact versus approximate attention

Everything above is exact attention: every allowed pair is scored, and the softmax is computed exactly (up to rounding). The project also studies methods that change the computation:

  • Restricted attention (local window, block sparse) still uses the exact softmax but forbids many pairs, as if a fixed mask were applied.
  • Linear attention replaces exp(q·k) with a different similarity that can be computed faster. It is not softmax attention at all, just a related function.

These are different research questions. For exact methods we ask "do they compute the same thing, and how fast?" For approximate methods we ask "how fast, and what do we lose?" (Chapter 10).

Key points to remember

  • Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V; each output is a weighted average of value vectors.
  • QKᵀ is an L × L table, the source of the quadratic cost.
  • Divide by √d so that scores have unit variance.
  • Masks set forbidden scores to −∞. Causal: j ≤ i. Fully-masked rows output 0 by project policy.
  • Our tensors are [B, H, L, d]. Heads are independent attentions.
  • RoPE makes attention depend on relative position. That helps the model, and can also create shortcuts.

Chapter 5 — Why attention is "quadratic", and what that does and does not mean

What you will learn: exactly which parts of attention grow with L², by counting; how big the score tables get; the difference between time, auxiliary memory, training memory and memory traffic; what each algorithm family changes; and why "quadratic" is only the start of the story.

5.1 Counting the work

For one head with L tokens and head dimension d:

Step What it computes Size of result Arithmetic
S = Q Kᵀ L × L dot products of length d L² numbers 2·L²·d FLOPs
scale, mask, max, exp, sum, divide elementwise on S L² numbers each about 4·L² operations
O = P V L weighted averages over L values of length d L·d numbers 2·L²·d FLOPs

Total ≈ 4·L²·d multiply-add FLOPs per head, plus O(L²) cheaper elementwise operations. With a batch of B texts and H heads, multiply by B·H. In big-O: time O(B·H·L²·d).

The inputs and outputs (Q, K, V, O) hold only 4·B·H·L·d numbers, which is linear in L. The quadratic part is the intermediate score and probability tables.

5.2 How big the tables get

The project's complexity model (python lab.py complexity, labeled THEORETICAL) gives, for B = 1, H = 4, d = 64, fp32:

L logits evaluated (all exact methods) matmul GFLOP per forward naive: forward allocations naive: saved for backward
1,024 4.2 million 1.07 49 MiB 48 MiB
4,096 67 million 17.2 772 MiB 768 MiB
16,384 1.07 billion 275 12,304 MiB (12 GiB) 12,288 MiB

Quadrupling L multiplies all of these by 16. At 16,384 tokens, one forward call of one attention layer written naively would need 12 GiB of temporary memory, which is most of this laptop's RAM. That is the practical meaning of "quadratic".

Compare the inputs: q, k, v, out at L = 16,384 are 4 × 4 × 16384 × 64 × 4 bytes = 64 MiB. The temporary tables are 190 times larger than the actual inputs and outputs.

5.3 Four different kinds of "memory cost"

Confusing these is the most common mistake in discussions of efficient attention. The project keeps them separate:

  1. Auxiliary memory of one forward call: temporary tensors that exist only during the call. Naive: O(L²). Tiled and fused: O(tile² + L·d).
  2. Memory saved for the backward pass: what autograd keeps alive between forward and backward when training. Naive: the L² probability tables. Autograd-tiled: also L² in total, because it keeps every tile. Recompute: only O(L) statistics.
  3. Total training memory of a model: parameters, gradients, optimizer state (AdamW keeps 2 extra numbers per parameter), activations of every layer, plus the attention terms above.
  4. Memory traffic: how many bytes travel between RAM and the caches. This is not storage at all; it is movement. A method can allocate little and still move a lot, or the other way round. Traffic is what FlashAttention's analysis is about (Chapter 8) and what largely decides speed (Chapter 3).

Chapter 13 explains which of these the project measures (1 and 2 directly, and process-level memory), which it estimates (all, in theory), and which it cannot measure directly (4, which would need hardware counters).

5.4 What each family of algorithms changes

Family Time Auxiliary memory Computes exact attention?
Naive / materializing O(L²d) O(L²) yes
Tiled / fused (FlashAttention idea) O(L²d), unchanged O(tile² + Ld) yes
Local window (width w) O(L·w·d) O(L·w) no: only nearby pairs
Block sparse (k blocks per row) O(L·k·b·d) O(L·k·b) no: only selected blocks
Linear attention O(L·d²) O(d²) (non-causal) no: a different function

Two things stand out:

  • Tiling attacks memory, not arithmetic. Every exact algorithm must look at every allowed pair, because every output depends on every pair. Tiling only decides where the scores live: in small, cache-resident tiles instead of a giant table. Chapter 14 confirms this experimentally: every exact method's time grows like L^1.9–2.1, while the tiled methods' memory grows like L^0.8.
  • Only methods that change the function can change the time complexity. Local, block-sparse and linear attention are faster asymptotically because they compute something different. Whether that difference matters is a quality question (Chapters 16 and 18).

5.5 Why "quadratic" is only the start of the story

Big-O hides constant factors, and real performance depends on:

  • Memory traffic (Chapter 3): the number of passes over large tables, not just their count.
  • Dispatch overhead: Python-level loops pay microseconds per operation.
  • Parallel efficiency: how well the work splits across threads.
  • Hardware: cache sizes, vector width, supported number formats.

These factors explain every "surprising" result in this book:

  • the C++ fused kernel is 3× faster than the Python tiled code, despite the same complexity (Chapter 14);
  • local-window attention, which is O(L), is slower than exact attention below about 2,048 tokens (Chapter 15);
  • adding threads makes the Python tiled code slower (Chapter 15).

Key points to remember

  • Exact attention: 4·L²·d FLOPs per head; quadratic time always.
  • Naive auxiliary memory: about 3·L² numbers. At L = 16,384 and 4 heads that is 12 GiB.
  • Separate auxiliary memory, saved-for-backward memory, total training memory and memory traffic.
  • Tiling reduces memory, not arithmetic. Only changing the function reduces arithmetic.
  • Measured speed depends on constants, traffic, dispatch, threads and hardware, not only on big-O.

Chapter 6 — A guided tour of the codebase, and how the project started

What you will learn: what was on the machine on day one and how it was checked; how the project is organized and why; the single calling convention that ties everything together; the registry of algorithms; and where every kind of output is stored.

6.1 Day one: the audit

The project started in an empty folder (not even a git repository) inside OneDrive on the Desktop. The first job was to verify the environment rather than trust the brief:

What was checked How Finding
Folder contents ls -la, find empty
CPU PowerShell Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor Ryzen 5 7530U (the brief said 5300U), 6 cores / 12 threads
RAM Win32_ComputerSystem, psutil 16.4 GB total, only 0.86–1.27 GB free at the time
GPU Win32_VideoController AMD Radeon integrated graphics, no CUDA
Disk Get-PSDrive C 30 GB free (not the 500 GB the brief described)
Python python --version, py -0p 3.13.3
Packages import each torch 2.10.0+cpu, numpy 2.5.2, scipy, pandas 3.0.0, matplotlib 3.10.8, streamlit 1.58, pytest 8.3.4, psutil 7.2.2, pyyaml
PyTorch internals torch.__config__.parallel_info(), torch.backends.cpu.get_cpu_capability() MKL and oneDNN present, OpenMP, 6 intra-op threads by default, capability AVX2
Attention kernels profiler on scaled_dot_product_attention CPU SDPA runs aten::_scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu (Chapter 9)
Fully-masked rows tiny experiment SDPA returns zeros, a naive softmax returns NaN (Chapter 7)
Profiler memory events tiny experiment [memory] events carry nbytes() and timestamps, so a peak can be reconstructed (Chapter 13)
Python start-up cost timed import torch 5.5 s cold, so running every benchmark in a fresh process would be expensive (Chapter 13)

Three decisions came straight out of the audit:

  1. Everything must work on CPU, and must never be described as a GPU result.
  2. Every benchmark needs a memory guard, because free RAM was below 1.3 GB.
  3. The project would not be installed into the system Python. A tiny launcher, lab.py, adds src/ to the import path, so python lab.py ... works from a fresh checkout. (pip install -e . also works, but is optional.)

What actually happened: the free disk space (30 GB) and the CPU model (7530U) both differed from the brief. They are recorded in the documentation as found, not as described. Later, the free RAM and the CPU load turned out to change minute by minute because of other programs. That discovery reshaped the benchmarking methodology (Chapters 13 and 22).

6.2 The layout

Beyond Quadratic Attention/
├── lab.py                      launcher: python lab.py <command>
├── pyproject.toml              package metadata + pytest settings
├── README.md                   quick start and command list
├── src/attention_lab/          the library (≈ 4,450 lines)
│   ├── algorithms/             the 8 attention implementations + shared mask logic + registry
│   ├── correctness/            error metrics, tolerance policy, correctness laboratory
│   ├── complexity/             theoretical cost model
│   ├── benchmarking/           environment capture, timing, memory, load monitor, runner, scheduler
│   ├── tasks/                  retrieval probes + synthetic token tasks
│   ├── models/                 tiny Transformer with pluggable attention
│   ├── training/               training loop + multi-backend task experiments
│   ├── diagnostics/            instrumented training for the MQAR investigation
│   ├── reporting/              results → tables, fitted exponents, markdown reports
│   ├── visualization/          matplotlib figures from measured data
│   ├── cli/                    command-line interface
│   └── ui/                     Streamlit web interface
├── tests/                      unit / numerical / integration / scientific / perf_smoke
├── scripts/                    diagnose_recall.py, summarize_diag.py
├── experiments/
│   ├── configs/                YAML specifications of every benchmark sweep
│   ├── results/<run>/          raw results: results.jsonl + meta.json  (never edited by hand)
│   ├── reports/<run>/          generated summary.md, CSV tables, PNG figures
│   ├── diagnostics/mqar_v2/    logs of the MQAR diagnostic experiments
│   └── checkpoints/            saved model weights (git-ignored)
└── docs/                       guides, results, this book

The Python source is about 5,600 lines in total, including tests and scripts. The largest files are the CLI (360 lines), the benchmark runner (241), the tiled attention (230) and the reporting module (227).

Why this separation? The brief demanded that algorithms, benchmarks, model integration and UI be kept apart. The practical reason is trust: an algorithm file contains only computation (no timing, no file writing), so it can be tested in isolation, and a benchmark cannot accidentally change what it measures.

6.3 One calling convention for everything

Every attention implementation, exact or approximate, is called the same way:

out = method(q, k, v, causal=False, key_padding_mask=None, **params)
# q: [B, H, L, d]   k: [B, H, L, d]   v: [B, H, L, dv]   →   out: [B, H, L, dv]

params holds method-specific knobs: q_tile and kv_tile for the tiled methods, window for local attention, block_size and friends for block-sparse attention, chunk for linear attention. Because the signature is shared, the benchmark runner, the correctness laboratory, the probes, the Transformer model and the UI are each written once and switch algorithms by name.

6.4 The registry

In the code: src/attention_lab/algorithms/registry.py

The registry maps each name to an AttentionMethod record:

AttentionMethod(
    name="tiled",
    fn=tiled_attention,
    family="exact",                       # or "restricted-softmax" or "different-kernel"
    computes="softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d) + M) V",
    implementation="Python-loop online-softmax tiling; autograd through the loop ...",
    default_params={"q_tile": 128, "kv_tile": 128},
    supports_dense_mask=True, ...
)

The family and computes fields make the scientific status of each method explicit. Reports and the UI use family to decide whether an output difference should be called an error (exact methods) or a deviation (approximate methods). This matters because, for example, linear attention's difference from softmax is not a mistake: it is a different function (Chapter 10).

The eight registered names: naive, sdpa_math, sdpa_flash_cpu, tiled, tiled_recompute, local_window, block_sparse, linear_elu.

6.5 Where outputs go

  • Raw results (experiments/results/<timestamp>_<name>/): results.jsonl holds one JSON object per configuration, including skipped and failed ones with a reason. meta.json holds the full spec and the environment. These files are the evidence and are never edited by hand.
  • Reports (experiments/reports/<same name>/): generated from the raw results by python lab.py report <run>: summary.md, summary.csv, exponents.csv and PNG figures.
  • Documentation (docs/): results.md collects the findings and names the run behind every number.

Keeping raw data, generated reports and interpretation separate means any number in this book can be traced back: book → docs/results.md → run name → results.jsonl line.

Key points to remember

  • The audit found a different CPU (7530U), little free RAM and no GPU, and the design followed from that.
  • Algorithms contain only computation. Benchmarks, models, probes and UI call them by name.
  • Shared signature: fn(q, k, v, causal=..., key_padding_mask=..., **params) on [B, H, L, d] tensors.
  • The registry labels each method's family, so errors and deviations are never confused.
  • Raw results → reports → docs: every number is traceable.

Chapter 7 — Implementation A: the reference ("naive") attention and the mask system

What you will learn: why a project like this needs a slow, obvious reference implementation; how the reference is written, line by line; how masks are defined once and shared by every algorithm; the fully-masked-row problem and how a policy was chosen; input validation; and how the reference itself is tested.

7.1 Why start with a slow implementation?

The first principle of the project was correctness before performance: an "optimization" that silently computes the wrong function is not an optimization. Every other algorithm is judged by comparing it with something we trust, so that thing must be as simple and transparent as possible. The reference (naive_attention) is written to be read, not to be fast. It literally builds the full L × L tables.

7.2 The code, step by step

In the code: src/attention_lab/algorithms/naive.py, function naive_attention.

shp = validate_qkv(q, k, v)                     # check shapes, dtypes, devices
sc = default_scale(shp.d, scale)                # 1/sqrt(d) unless told otherwise
spec = MaskSpec(shp, mask=mask, key_padding_mask=key_padding_mask, causal=causal, device=q.device)

s = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) * sc   # [B,H,Lq,Lk]   the quadratic table
allowed, additive = spec.tile(0, shp.Lq, 0, shp.Lk)
s = apply_tile_mask(s, allowed, additive)       # forbidden pairs -> -inf

m = safe_row_max(s)                             # [B,H,Lq,1]    row maximum (stable softmax)
e = torch.exp(s - m)                            # [B,H,Lq,Lk]   second quadratic table
l = e.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)                 # [B,H,Lq,1]    row sums
l_safe = torch.where(l == 0, torch.ones_like(l), l)
p = e / l_safe                                  # [B,H,Lq,Lk]   third quadratic table
out = torch.matmul(p, v)                        # [B,H,Lq,dv]

Every line maps to one step of Chapter 4's formula. Notice the three L × L tensors s, e and p. At the peak of the call they all exist at once, which is why the theory model predicts naive forward memory as "3 score tables + output". The measured memory matched to within 0.1 MiB (Chapter 14).

naive_attention(..., return_lse=True) also returns the log-sum-exp of each row, m + log(l). The tiled implementations store exactly this per-row statistic for their backward pass (Chapter 8), and tests compare the two.

7.3 The stable softmax and the detached maximum

safe_row_max (in base.py) does two things:

m = s.detach().amax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
return torch.where(torch.isneginf(m), torch.zeros_like(m), m)
  1. Detach. The softmax result does not depend on which constant is subtracted (Chapter 2), so in exact arithmetic the gradient flowing "through" m cancels out. Detaching tells autograd not to compute that cancelling term, which avoids a little extra rounding noise.
  2. Replace −∞ with 0. If every score in a row is −∞ (a fully-masked row), the maximum is −∞, and s − m would be −∞ − (−∞) = NaN. Using 0 instead gives exp(−∞ − 0) = 0, so the whole row of e is zero, l is zero, and the l_safe line divides by 1 instead of 0. The output row is zero.

7.4 The fully-masked row: choosing a policy

Mathematically, a query with no allowed keys has an undefined attention output (0/0). Implementations disagree about what to return. Some produce NaN, which then spreads through the network like a poison.

What actually happened: during the audit, two tiny experiments were run. A plain torch.softmax over a row of −∞ returned [nan, nan, nan, nan]. PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention on CPU, with a mask that removed a whole row, returned a zero vector for that row, and the gradients contained no NaN. Both of PyTorch's CPU backends (the fused flash kernel and the math kernel) were checked with boolean and with additive masks, and all returned zeros. The project therefore adopted the same policy, fully-masked rows produce zero output and zero gradient, wrote it into the docstring of base.py, and tested it for every exact method (test_fully_masked_rows_and_padding, test_fully_masked_rows_give_zero_output_and_zero_grad).

7.5 Masks are defined in exactly one place: MaskSpec

In the code: src/attention_lab/algorithms/base.py, class MaskSpec.

Masks are easy to get subtly wrong. Is True "keep" or "remove"? Is causal "j ≤ i" or "j < i"? What happens when the query and key lengths differ? To avoid each algorithm answering these questions differently, all mask logic lives in one class, and the semantics are written at the top of base.py:

  • boolean mask: True means the pair takes part (the same convention as PyTorch SDPA);
  • float mask: added to the scaled scores, where −∞ removes the pair; +∞ and NaN are rejected;
  • key_padding_mask [B, Lk]: True = real token;
  • causal=True: query i may attend key j iff j ≤ i (top-left aligned, the same as SDPA's is_causal).

The key design idea: algorithms never ask for "the mask". They ask for the mask of the tile they are about to compute:

allowed, additive = spec.tile(qs, qe, ks, ke)   # queries [qs, qe) × keys [ks, ke)

For a causal mask, the tile is built on the fly from two small arange vectors (kj <= qi). For a user-supplied dense mask, the tile is a slice of a broadcast view, so no L × L copy is made. This is what lets the tiled algorithm support arbitrary masks while still never materializing an L × L table.

spec.tile_fully_masked_by_causality(qs, qe, ks) tells a tiled loop when a whole tile lies above the diagonal, so it can skip it entirely (Chapter 8).

Causal alignment when lengths differ. "Top-left" means query 0 lines up with key 0. When generating text with a cache of previous keys (Lq < Lk), the usual intent is "bottom-right" (the last query lines up with the last key). The project deliberately implements only top-left, matching SDPA, and documents that you need an explicit mask for the other convention. A test (test_causal_is_top_left_aligned_like_sdpa) pins this behaviour against PyTorch.

7.6 Input validation

validate_qkv rejects, with a clear message:

  • tensors that are not 4-D [B, H, L, d];
  • non-floating-point dtypes, or q/k/v with different dtypes or devices;
  • mismatched batch or head dimensions; q and k with different head dimensions; k and v with different lengths;
  • zero-sized dimensions.

default_scale rejects non-positive scales. MaskSpec rejects masks that cannot broadcast to [B, H, Lq, Lk], padding masks with the wrong shape or dtype, and additive masks containing +∞ or NaN. Each rejection has a test in tests/unit/test_base_and_naive.py.

7.7 How the reference itself is tested

A reference must be checked against something independent. The tests compare it with a separate formulation, softmax(QKᵀ·scale + bias) @ V using torch.softmax (textbook() in the test file), and with PyTorch's own SDPA:

Test What it proves
test_matches_textbook_formula_and_default_scale same output as an independent formula, to 1e-12
test_scale_is_one_over_sqrt_d default scale is exactly 1/√d
test_rows_of_probabilities_sum_to_one probabilities are non-negative and sum to 1
test_bool_mask_true_means_attend with only key 2 allowed, every output equals v₂
test_additive_mask_is_added_to_scaled_logits float masks are biases
test_causal_is_top_left_aligned_like_sdpa causal = tril mask = PyTorch's is_causal
test_key_padding_mask_excludes_padded_keys changing padded values to 10⁶ changes nothing
test_masks_combine_by_intersection mask + causal + padding = their logical AND
test_lse_matches_logsumexp the returned LSE equals torch.logsumexp
test_gradients_match_textbook, test_gradcheck_naive gradients are correct (including finite-difference gradcheck)

torch.autograd.gradcheck deserves a word. It perturbs each input by a tiny amount in float64, measures how the output changes (a numerical derivative), and compares that with the gradient computed by autograd. It is the gold standard for "is my backward pass right?".

Key points to remember

  • The reference is deliberately simple and builds three L × L tables.
  • The stable softmax subtracts a detached row max, with −∞ replaced by 0 for empty rows.
  • Fully-masked rows output zero, a policy chosen by checking what PyTorch's CPU kernels do.
  • MaskSpec defines mask semantics once and serves masks per tile, without building L × L masks.
  • Causal is top-left aligned, like SDPA.
  • The reference is tested against an independent formula, PyTorch SDPA, and finite-difference gradients.

Chapter 8 — Implementation B: tiled exact attention and the online softmax

What you will learn: the central trick of FlashAttention, called online softmax: how to compute an exact softmax-weighted average while seeing the scores one tile at a time; a worked numerical example; the proof that it is exact; how the project implements it; why letting autograd differentiate through it does not save training memory; and how a custom "recompute" backward pass fixes that.

8.1 The problem

Naive attention builds the whole row of scores s₁ … s_L for a query before applying softmax, because the softmax denominator Σ exp(sⱼ) needs all of them. The question is whether the scores can be processed in small tiles (chunks of keys) so that the full row never exists, and still get the exact answer.

The difficulty is that the stable softmax subtracts the row maximum, and we only know the true maximum after seeing every tile.

8.2 The idea: keep three running numbers and fix them up when the maximum changes

For one query row, while streaming over tiles, keep:

  • m: the largest score seen so far;
  • l: the sum of exp(sⱼ − m) over keys seen so far (the denominator, relative to the current m);
  • acc: the sum of exp(sⱼ − m) · vⱼ over keys seen so far (the numerator, also relative to m).

When a new tile arrives with scores S and values V_tile:

U1   m_new = max(m, max(S))              new running maximum
U2   α     = exp(m − m_new)              how much to shrink the old sums (≤ 1)
U3   P     = exp(S − m_new)              this tile's weights, relative to m_new
U4   l     = α · l   + sum(P)            rescale the old denominator, add the new terms
U5   acc   = α · acc + P · V_tile        rescale the old numerator, add the new terms
     m     = m_new

At the end: output = acc / l, and the log-sum-exp is lse = m + log(l).

The only "trick" is U2. Old sums were computed relative to the old maximum. Multiplying by exp(m − m_new) re-bases them to the new maximum, because exp(s − m) · exp(m − m_new) = exp(s − m_new).

8.3 A worked example

One query, four keys, scores s = [1, 3, 2, 5], scalar values v = [10, 20, 30, 40], tiles of 2 keys.

Start: m = −∞, l = 0, acc = 0.

Tile 0 (scores [1, 3], values [10, 20]):

m_new = max(−∞, 3) = 3
α     = exp(−∞ − 3) = 0
P     = [exp(1−3), exp(3−3)] = [0.135335, 1]
l     = 0·0 + 1.135335 = 1.135335
acc   = 0·0 + 0.135335·10 + 1·20 = 21.353353

Tile 1 (scores [2, 5], values [30, 40]): the maximum rises from 3 to 5, so the old sums shrink:

m_new = max(3, 5) = 5
α     = exp(3 − 5) = 0.135335
P     = [exp(2−5), exp(5−5)] = [0.049787, 1]
l     = 0.135335 · 1.135335 + 1.049787 = 1.203438
acc   = 0.135335 · 21.353353 + 0.049787·30 + 1·40 = 44.383474

Result: acc / l = 36.880566, and lse = 5 + log(1.203438) = 5.185182.

Check with the direct formula: weights exp([1,3,2,5]) / Σ and the weighted average of [10,20,30,40] give 36.880566, with lse = log Σ exp = 5.185182. They are identical (to 15 digits in this calculation).

8.4 Why it is exactly right (the proof)

Invariant: after processing tiles 1..t, l = Σ_{seen j} exp(sⱼ − m) and acc = Σ_{seen j} exp(sⱼ − m) vⱼ, where m is the max over seen keys.

  • It holds at the start (empty sums are 0; m = −∞).
  • If it holds before a tile, then α · l = Σ_old exp(sⱼ − m)·exp(m − m_new) = Σ_old exp(sⱼ − m_new), and U4 adds exactly the new terms Σ_tile exp(sⱼ − m_new). So it holds after. The same argument works for acc.
  • At the end, acc / l = Σ exp(sⱼ − m) vⱼ / Σ exp(sⱼ − m); the common exp(−m) cancels, leaving Σ exp(sⱼ) vⱼ / Σ exp(sⱼ), the softmax-weighted average. ∎

Tile order and tile sizes do not matter mathematically. A unit test streams the same row with five different splits ([10], [1]×10, [3,3,4], [7,1,2], [2,8]) and gets the same answer every time (test_streaming_equals_softmax_for_any_split).

Numerical safety. Every exponent is ≤ 0 (scores never exceed the running max), so nothing overflows. Even if a later tile is 1,000 larger, α = exp(−1000) = 0 simply discards the negligible old mass (test_update_handles_increasing_maxima_without_overflow). If all scores seen so far are masked (−∞), the code shifts by 0 instead of −∞ so that no NaN appears (test_update_handles_all_masked_first_tile).

8.5 The implementation

In the code: src/attention_lab/algorithms/tiled_exact.py.

The update rule is a standalone function, so that the documentation, the unit tests and the kernel all use the same code:

def online_softmax_update(m, l, acc, s, v_j):
    m_new = torch.maximum(m, s.detach().amax(dim=-1, keepdim=True))           # U1
    m_shift = torch.where(torch.isneginf(m_new), torch.zeros_like(m_new), m_new)
    alpha = torch.exp(m - m_shift)                                             # U2
    p = torch.exp(s - m_shift)                                                 # U3
    l = alpha * l + p.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True)                                # U4
    acc = alpha * acc + torch.matmul(p, v_j)                                   # U5
    return m_new, l, acc

The forward kernel, tiled_forward_kernel, loops over query tiles (outer loop, q_tile rows) and key tiles (inner loop, kv_tile keys). For each tile pair it computes a small q_tile × kv_tile score block, asks MaskSpec for that tile's mask, and applies the update. It works on whole [B, H, …] blocks at once, so all batches and heads advance together. Three details:

  • Ragged final tiles. If L is not a multiple of the tile size, the last tile is simply shorter (Python slicing handles it). Tests use awkward sizes such as L = 77 with tiles of 16 and 24.
  • Causal tile skipping. If a key tile starts after the last query of the current block, every pair is above the diagonal, and every later tile is too, so the inner loop breaks. For L = 64 with 16 × 16 tiles, 10 of 16 tiles are computed (test_causal_skips_tiles_above_diagonal).
  • fp32 accumulators for 16-bit inputs. If the inputs are bfloat16, the running m, l, acc and the score tiles are computed in fp32 (_acc_dtype). FlashAttention does the same. Chapter 11 shows this single choice is the difference between 0.3 % and 38 % error.

What actually happened: the update function was originally written inline inside the kernel. Halfway through the first benchmark sweep it was moved into the standalone online_softmax_update, so that tests could exercise it alone. Because the sweep's worker processes import the code fresh, later configurations of that sweep ran the refactored version. The operations were identical, plus one Python function call per tile, which is negligible. This was noted, and that sweep's timings were later discarded anyway, for a different reason (Chapter 13).

8.6 The backward pass: where tiling alone fails

Training needs gradients. The simplest option, tiled_attention, lets PyTorch's autograd differentiate straight through the Python loop. That gives correct gradients (tests confirm it to 1e-15 in fp64). But autograd must keep every tile's intermediate tensors (each P, each exp output) alive until the backward pass. Added up over all tiles, that is again O(L²) memory. The forward pass was memory-efficient; training is not.

The measurement in Chapter 14 shows it plainly. The forward-plus-backward memory of the autograd-tiled version grows with exponent 1.72 in L (76 MiB at L = 2048), compared with 0.75 for the recompute version (9.9 MiB).

8.7 The fix: recompute instead of store

tiled_attention_recompute is a custom torch.autograd.Function, a piece of code with a hand-written backward:

  • Forward: run the same tiled kernel, but save only Q, K, V, the output O and the per-row lse = m + log(l). That is O(L·d) memory, nothing quadratic.
  • Backward: loop over key tiles (outer) and query tiles (inner). Recompute each score tile S = Q_i K_jᵀ · scale, and recover the exact probabilities as P = exp(S − lse). Because lse is the exact log-normalizer of each row, this gives exactly the softmax weights, with no need to know the maximum again.

The gradient formulas, derived in docs/attention_math.md §4, are:

D   = rowsum(dO ∘ O)            computed once, O(L·d)
dV += Pᵀ dO
dP  = dO Vᵀ
dS  = P ∘ (dP − D)
dQ += dS K · scale
dK += dSᵀ Q · scale

The trick is in D. The softmax Jacobian needs Σ_k P_ik dP_ik for each row, which looks as if it needs the whole row of P. But dP_ik = dO_i · V_k and O_i = Σ_k P_ik V_k, so the sum equals dO_i · O_i, which can be computed from O and dO alone. The same structure appears in FlashAttention-2's backward pass (Dao, 2023).

The cost of the trade: one extra Q Kᵀ per tile, about 25 % more matmul FLOPs in the backward pass (10·L²·d instead of 8·L²·d). The benefit: saved memory falls from O(L²) to O(L·d).

Validation: torch.autograd.gradcheck on a causal, padded, ragged-tile case (test_gradcheck_tiled_recompute_custom_backward), plus comparisons with naive gradients across 49–57 cases per dtype in the correctness laboratory. All pass.

What actually happened: a measured surprise. The recompute version does more arithmetic, yet it was faster than the autograd version at every length from 512 tokens upward (980 ms vs 1,847 ms at L = 2048 on one thread), and faster than naive (1,411 ms). Allocating and keeping hundreds of MiB of tiles costs more than recomputing them. This is a CPU echo of FlashAttention's main argument: on modern hardware, moving memory is often more expensive than arithmetic (Chapter 14).

8.8 What this implementation is not

It is not FlashAttention. FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) is a single fused GPU kernel that keeps tiles in on-chip SRAM and never writes scores to main memory. Our Python version runs each line as a separate PyTorch operation, each of which reads and writes its operands through the cache hierarchy. It reproduces the algorithm and its memory behaviour, not the hardware efficiency. Chapter 9 introduces the fused CPU kernel that PyTorch provides, which does exploit the hardware, and Chapter 14 compares them.

Key points to remember

  • Online softmax keeps m, l and acc per row and rescales by α = exp(m_old − m_new) when the max grows.
  • It is exactly equal to softmax in exact arithmetic, for any tile order or size.
  • Worked example: scores [1,3,2,5] and values [10,20,30,40] give 36.880566 by both methods.
  • Tiles are processed in [B,H] blocks; ragged tiles are fine; causal tiles above the diagonal are skipped.
  • 16-bit inputs use fp32 accumulators.
  • Autograd through the loop makes training memory O(L²) again (measured exponent 1.72).
  • The recompute backward stores only O, lse (O(L·d)), recomputes P = exp(S − lse), and uses D = rowsum(dO∘O).
  • Recompute does 25 % more backward FLOPs, yet measured faster than storing on this CPU.

Chapter 9 — Implementation C: PyTorch's built-in kernels and how we found out which one runs

What you will learn: what PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA) is; why "which kernel ran?" is a real question; how the profiler answered it; the two adapters the project registers; how masks are translated; and why the CPU "flash" kernel must not be called FlashAttention.

9.1 SDPA: one function, several implementations

PyTorch offers torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=None, is_causal=False, scale=None). Behind that single function, PyTorch chooses among several backends (implementations): FlashAttention-style kernels, "memory-efficient" kernels and cuDNN on CUDA GPUs, and a "math" fallback. You can force a backend with the context manager torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.X).

The PyTorch documentation (checked during the project) describes the optimized kernels in terms of the CUDA backend and says that other backends use the plain PyTorch implementation. On a CPU-only machine it was therefore unclear what would actually run.

9.2 Asking the profiler

The PyTorch profiler records every operator executed inside a with profile(...) block. During the audit, SDPA was run with each backend and mask type, and the operator names were collected:

Forced backend Operators observed
default (none forced) aten::_scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu (+ _backward)
SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION aten::_scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu (+ _backward)
SDPBackend.MATH aten::_scaled_dot_product_attention_math (backward = ordinary ops)

This was true with is_causal=True, with a boolean mask and with an additive float mask. So this CPU build of PyTorch has a dedicated fused "flash" kernel for CPUs and uses it by default. A research subagent then checked PyTorch's source: the operator is declared in native_functions.yaml, returns (output, logsumexp), and is selected by the CPU backend selector. It came in through a pull request that initially supported forward fp32 only. The docs sentence about "CUDA only" is out of date for CPU (recorded in docs/references.md).

The same experiment confirmed the fully-masked-row behaviour: both CPU backends return zeros (Chapter 7).

9.3 The two adapters

In the code: src/attention_lab/algorithms/sdpa.py.

_BACKENDS = {"flash": SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION, "math": SDPBackend.MATH}

def sdpa_attention(q, k, v, *, mask=None, key_padding_mask=None, causal=False, scale=None, backend="flash"):
    ...
    attn_mask, is_causal = _sdpa_mask(spec)
    with sdpa_kernel(_BACKENDS[backend]):
        return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, attn_mask=attn_mask, is_causal=is_causal, scale=sc)

Two registry entries use it: sdpa_flash_cpu (forced flash) and sdpa_math (forced math). Forcing the backend means every benchmark row states which kernel ran, instead of relying on an automatic choice that might change between PyTorch versions.

Mask translation (_sdpa_mask). SDPA does not accept attn_mask and is_causal together, and it has no separate padding mask. The adapter therefore:

  • passes is_causal=True with no mask tensor when causality is the only mask (the cheapest case);
  • otherwise builds the combined mask at its broadcast shape: a padding mask alone stays [B, 1, 1, L]; anything combined with causality becomes […, L, L] (an O(L²) boolean, a documented cost of the adapter, not of the kernel);
  • merges boolean and additive masks into one additive mask (additive.masked_fill(~allowed, −∞)).

9.4 What the flash CPU kernel does, and what it is not

The ATen CPU kernel processes blocks of queries against blocks of keys inside one C++ function. Scaling, masking, the running max, exp, the running sums and the P·V accumulation all happen on small blocks held in cache. It uses vectorized exp, parallelizes over (batch, head, query block) with OpenMP, and stores the logsumexp for the backward pass. That is the same algorithm as Chapter 8, but fused: no intermediate ever goes to RAM, and there is no per-operation Python dispatch.

It is not the official FlashAttention library by Dao et al., which is a CUDA implementation for NVIDIA GPUs. The project never calls it FlashAttention. Its registry entry reads "PyTorch's fused tiled C++ CPU kernel; NOT the official FlashAttention CUDA library".

sdpa_math is PyTorch's own materializing implementation, essentially an optimized version of our naive reference.

9.5 How they compare (preview of Chapter 14)

Both adapters agree with the reference to about 1e-15 in fp64. On one thread at L = 4096 (forward), the fused kernel took 516 ms, against about 1,500 ms for naive, the math backend, and the Python tiled code. All four compute the same mathematics, so the factor of about 3 comes entirely from how the computation is executed.

Key points to remember

  • SDPA has several backends. On this CPU build, the default is a fused flash-style CPU kernel.
  • The profiler (operator names) is how we verified which kernel ran, instead of assuming.
  • sdpa_flash_cpu and sdpa_math force their backends, so results always name the kernel.
  • The adapter merges masks into SDPA's format, and combined causal+padding masks cost an L × L boolean.
  • The CPU flash kernel is PyTorch's own and must not be called "FlashAttention".

Chapter 10 — The approximate methods: local window, block sparse and linear attention

What you will learn: what each approximate method computes exactly (restricted softmax versus a different function); how each is implemented efficiently in PyTorch (the unfold trick, gathering active blocks, the associativity trick and chunked prefix sums); how each is verified against its own definition; and where each one's cost comes from.

10.1 Two kinds of "approximate"

  • Restricted softmax (local window, block sparse): exactly the softmax attention of Chapter 4, but with many pairs forbidden, as if a fixed mask were applied. Inside the allowed pairs everything is exact. What is lost is information: the forbidden pairs.
  • Different function (linear attention): replaces exp(q·k/√d) by another similarity. It is not softmax attention with an error; it is a different model.

The project verifies each method against its own exact definition. For restricted methods that is naive attention with the corresponding mask. For linear attention it is a slow, direct evaluation of the same formula. Their difference from full softmax attention is then measured separately and called deviation, never "error".

10.2 Local-window (sliding-window) attention

What it computes: query i may attend to key j only if i − w_left ≤ j ≤ i + w_right. With window = w non-causal, both sides are w; causal means [i − w, i]. This idea is used, for example, in Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020).

The naive way would waste the savings: build the full L × L table and mask most of it. That costs as much as full attention.

The project's way: chunks and unfold.

In the code: src/attention_lab/algorithms/local_window.py.

  1. Split the queries into chunks of C rows. Chunk c covers queries [cC, cC + C).
  2. Those queries can only see keys in [cC − w_l, cC + C + w_r), a span of S = C + w_l + w_r keys.
  3. Pad K and V with w_l zeros in front and w_r (plus padding to a multiple of C) behind, then call kp.unfold(2, S, C). That produces, as a strided view, all overlapping windows of S keys starting every C positions: a [B, H, nC, S, d] tensor.
  4. Compute scores chunk by chunk, all at once: [B, H, nC, C, d] @ [B, H, nC, d, S] → [B, H, nC, C, S].
  5. Build the band mask for a chunk: query row a and window slot b are allowed iff 0 ≤ b − a ≤ w_l + w_r. Also remove positions that fall in the padding (key_pos < 0 or ≥ L), and apply the padding mask after unfolding it in the same way.
  6. Stable softmax, multiply by the unfolded values, reshape back to [B, H, L, dv].

Fully vectorized, with no Python loop over positions. Scores evaluated: ⌈L/C⌉ · C · (C + w_l + w_r), which is linear in L. About C/(C + w_l + w_r) of them are masked waste; the default C ≈ w_l + w_r + 1 wastes about half.

Verified by: test_local_window_equals_band_masked_softmax, a grid of lengths (1, 5, 37, 64), windows (0, 1, 4, 16, 100), causal/non-causal and chunk sizes, comparing output and gradients with naive attention under the band mask, to 1e-12. A window as large as the sequence equals full attention.

10.3 Block-sparse attention

What it computes: cut the sequence into blocks of b tokens. A boolean layout layout[qb, kb] says whether query block qb may attend key block kb. The project's layout, in the spirit of BigBird (Zaheer et al., 2020), combines:

  • local: |qb − kb| ≤ local_blocks (causal: 0 ≤ qb − kb ≤ local_blocks);
  • global: the first global_blocks key blocks are visible to everyone, and (non-causal) the first query blocks see everything;
  • random: each query block also sees random_blocks extra key blocks, chosen with a fixed seed so the layout is reproducible.

In the code: src/attention_lab/algorithms/block_sparse.py — make_layout, block_sparse_attention.

Execution by gathering. For each query block, collect the indices of its active key blocks, pad every row to the widest row (K_max), and gather those key and value blocks into a dense [B, H, n_rows, K_max·b, d] tensor. Then compute exact softmax attention over just those keys: [B, H, n_rows, b, K_max·b] scores instead of [B, H, L, L]. Padded slots, padded positions (when L is not a multiple of b), padding-mask positions and (causal) pairs above the diagonal inside diagonal blocks are all masked.

Global rows are handled separately. A query block that sees every block would force K_max = n_blocks for all rows and make the whole computation dense. So rows with full coverage are computed against all keys directly, and the rest use the gather path.

Verified by: test_block_sparse_equals_layout_masked_softmax (lengths including ragged 77 and 130, five layout configurations, causal/non-causal, gradients) against naive attention with the layout expanded to an element mask. Also tested: the layout is causal when asked, always includes the diagonal and the global column, and is reproducible from its seed.

What actually happened: at short lengths a "sparse" layout can cover everything. With b = 8 at L = 32 there are only 4 blocks, and local ±1 + global block 0 + 1 random block already includes all of them. The layout keeps 528 of 528 causal pairs, which is full attention. This was discovered when block_sparse scored exactly like exact attention on the induction task. The book and the results flag those cells as "not evidence about sparsity" (Chapter 18). Likewise, the deviation measurements show 0 at L = 256 with b = 64.

10.4 Linear attention (elu + 1)

What it computes (Katharopoulos et al., 2020): pick a feature map φ(x) = elu(x) + 1 (applied to each entry; always positive), and define

out_i = Σ_j [φ(q_i)·φ(k_j)] v_j  /  Σ_j φ(q_i)·φ(k_j)

It looks like attention with weights φ(q)·φ(k) instead of exp(q·k/√d). It is not an approximation of softmax: elu + 1 is not designed to estimate exp in any sense.
