(Random-feature methods such as Performer do estimate it, but they are not implemented here.) Following the paper, φ is applied to q and k directly, with no 1/√d, and passing a scale raises an error.

Why it can be linear in L: associativity. Σ_j (φ(q_i)ᵀ φ(k_j)) v_jᵀ = φ(q_i)ᵀ (Σ_j φ(k_j) v_jᵀ). The bracket is a d × d matrix that does not depend on i. Compute it once (O(L·d²)) and reuse it for every query (O(L·d²)). No L × L table at all.

Causal is harder. Query i needs the prefix sum S_i = Σ_{j≤i} φ(k_j) v_jᵀ, a different d × d matrix for every position. Storing all of them would cost O(L·d²) memory. The project uses a chunked form:

  • inside each chunk of C tokens, compute the small C × C causal attention directly (quadratic, but only in C);
  • across chunks, keep one d × d summary per chunk, take exclusive prefix sums (each chunk sees only earlier chunks), and apply them to the chunk's queries.

The exclusive prefix is built as "zeros, then the cumulative sum shifted by one", rather than "cumulative sum minus own chunk", to avoid cancellation error. Padded or masked keys get φ(k) = 0, so they contribute nothing. The denominator gets + 1e-6 for safety (it is positive anyway, because φ > 0).

In the code: src/attention_lab/algorithms/linear.py — linear_attention and linear_attention_quadratic_reference.

Verified by: test_linear_chunked_equals_quadratic_definition (lengths 1–100, chunks 1–128, causal and padded, gradients) against the slow direct formula. Two more tests show it is not softmax attention, and that its outputs are convex combinations of values.

10.5 What each method costs, in theory

From complexity/theory.py, for B = 1, H = 4, L = 4096, d = 64 (theory, not measurement):

Method (default params) Logits evaluated Matmul GFLOP Forward allocations
exact methods 67.1 million 17.2 naive 772 MiB; flash 4.1 MiB; tiled 9.2 MiB
local_window (w = 64) 4.2 million 1.09 68.6 MiB
block_sparse (b = 32, 1 local, 1 global, 1 random) 3.1 million 0.80 79.8 MiB
linear_elu (non-causal) 0 0.27 12.1 MiB

Note that the approximate methods' theoretical allocations are already much larger than the fused exact kernel's, because they materialize their restricted score tables or gathered blocks. Chapter 15 confirms this by measurement.

Key points to remember

  • Local and block-sparse attention are exact softmax on a restricted set of pairs. Linear attention is a different function.
  • Each is verified against its own definition (masked naive, or the direct formula), including gradients.
  • Local window: chunks + unfold + band mask, O(L·(C + 2w)) scores, about half of them masked waste.
  • Block sparse: layout (local + global + random), gather active blocks, pad to K_max, global rows done densely.
  • At short lengths a sparse layout may be dense (L = 32, b = 8 covers everything).
  • Linear: associativity gives O(L·d²); causal uses chunked exclusive prefix sums of d × d states.

Chapter 11 — The numerical-correctness laboratory

What you will learn: how to decide whether two implementations "compute the same thing" when floating point never gives exact equality; the metrics the project uses and why; the comparison protocol; the tolerance policy; and the two investigations that changed that policy, each started by a failing check and ended by finding the real cause.

11.1 Three meanings of "the same"

Notion Meaning
Mathematical equivalence equal in exact real-number arithmetic (proved on paper, e.g. Chapter 8)
Numerical equivalence equal within a tolerance justified by the number format and the operations involved
Bitwise equality the exact same bits

Different summation orders give different roundings (Chapter 3), so two correct implementations are generally not bitwise equal. A test pins this: naive and tiled outputs in fp32 differ by under 1e-5, but are not bitwise equal (test_numerical_vs_bitwise_equality_are_distinct_notions). If two mathematically equivalent implementations are not numerically equivalent, something is wrong: a bug, an instability, or a tolerance that does not fit the situation.

11.2 The metrics

In the code: src/attention_lab/correctness/metrics.py, function compare.

For an output x and a reference r (both converted to fp64):

  • max_abs: the largest absolute difference;
  • mean_abs: the mean absolute difference;
  • max_abs_normalized = max|x − r| / max|r|: the number the tolerances are checked against. Attention outputs are weighted averages of values, so max|r| is the natural scale;
  • rel_fro = ‖x − r‖ / ‖r‖: a global relative error that is robust to near-zero entries;
  • max_rel: elementwise relative error with an explicit floor. Entries where |r| ≤ 10⁻³ · max|r| are excluded, and the excluded fraction is reported. Without the floor, a reference entry of 10⁻¹² makes any rounding difference look like a 100 % error;
  • cosine: cosine similarity of the flattened outputs;
  • nan_count, inf_count;
  • bitwise_equal.

11.3 The protocol for one comparison

In the code: src/attention_lab/correctness/lab.py, evaluate_case.

  1. Draw q, k, v in fp64 from a seeded generator; multiply q and k by magnitude.
  2. Round them to the test dtype (fp32, bf16, …).
  3. The reference is naive attention in fp64 applied to the already-rounded inputs. That way the unavoidable error of rounding the inputs is not blamed on the algorithm.
  4. Run the method in the test dtype, for forward output and for gradients against a fixed random upstream gradient.
  5. Compute the metrics, look up the tolerance, record pass or fail.

The default matrix (default_cases) covers lengths 1, 7, 64, 129 (quick) plus 512 and 1024 (full); head dimensions 8–128; fp64, fp32 and bf16; causal and non-causal; tile sizes 32 × 48, which deliberately do not divide the lengths; input magnitudes 0.01 to 30; batch/head shapes (1,1) and (3,5); random key padding; and fully-masked rows. The full run made 795 comparisons (python lab.py correctness --full, run 20261011-194506_correctness).

11.4 The tolerance policy, and how it got that way

The current policy, against max_abs_normalized:

  • fp64: forward 1e-12, gradients 1e-10.
  • fp32: forward 2e-5, gradients 2e-4, or 4·u·max|S| (forward) / 16·u·max|S| (gradients) if larger, where max|S| is the largest logit and u = 2⁻²⁴.
  • bf16 / fp16: at most 2 × the error of a mixed-precision baseline plus a small slack (4e-3 forward, 1.6e-2 gradients for bf16). The baseline is naive attention computed in fp32 on the same rounded inputs, with results rounded to bf16.

Neither of the two non-obvious parts was in the first version. Both came from failures that were investigated rather than "fixed" by loosening.

Investigation 1: the bf16 baseline that was too lenient

First version: the bf16 tolerance was "2 × the error of naive attention computed in bf16". The reasoning was that low-precision methods should be no worse than the obvious low-precision implementation.

What the run showed: all methods passed, but the naive-in-bf16 baseline's own error was huge and grew with input magnitude. The breakdown (L = 96, d = 32):

input magnitude naive, all in bf16: fwd error tiled / SDPA (fp32 accumulators): fwd error
1 ~0.005 ~0.002
3 0.059 ~0.002
10 0.147 ~0.002
30 (full run) 0.377 ~0.003

Gradient errors were worse, up to 0.68 at magnitude 10 and 2.24 at magnitude 30.

Cause: at magnitude 10 the logits are in the hundreds. bf16 has 8 significant bits, so neighbouring representable numbers near 256 are 1 apart, and a logit can be off by up to 0.5. The softmax weight exp(s − m) is then off by up to e^0.5 ≈ 1.65×. The kernels that keep logits and running sums in fp32 do not suffer this.

Why the first policy was wrong: "2 × a 15 % error" accepts almost anything. A tolerance based on a bad baseline is meaningless.

Fix: use a mixed-precision baseline whose error is essentially the unavoidable rounding of the output to bf16 (about 2–3e-3). Under the new policy every fp32-accumulating method passes, and naive-in-bf16 fails 14 of 53 cases. That is now reported as a finding, not hidden: computing attention entirely in bf16 is inaccurate at realistic logit scales, which is why FlashAttention and the CPU kernel keep these values in fp32. A regression test pins it (test_finding_naive_in_pure_bfloat16_degrades_with_logit_magnitude).

Investigation 2: the fp32 "failure" that was the dtype's own floor

What happened: after the bf16 fix, one test failed: sdpa_flash_cpu in fp32 at input magnitude 10 had forward error 2.04e-5, against a tolerance of 2e-5.

The easy move would have been to change 2e-5 to 3e-5. Instead a hypothesis was formed. A logit s in fp32 can only be stored to about u·|s| absolute precision, and that becomes a relative error in its softmax weight of the same size. If so, the error should scale with the largest logit, for every implementation, including the naive formula. Measured (L = 64, d = 32, fp32), error divided by u·max|S|:

input magnitude max|S| naive sdpa_math sdpa_flash_cpu tiled
1 4.6 1.3 1.5 1.4 1.1
3 41 0.6 0.7 0.6 0.6
10 459 0.7 0.2 0.7 0.2
30 4135 0.1 0.2 0.1 0.1

At magnitude 10, the naive formula in fp32 had exactly the same error, 2.04e-5, as the fused kernel. The error tracked the logit scale for every implementation. (It saturates at magnitude 30 because the softmax becomes nearly one-hot and stops being sensitive.)

Conclusion: not a kernel bug, but the fp32 floor for large logits. Fix: add the term derived from the error model, 4·u·max|S|, which only matters for large logits. The fixed 2e-5 threshold still applies to ordinary inputs. A regression test pins the evidence (test_finding_fp32_error_floor_scales_with_logit_magnitude_for_every_implementation).

11.5 Results of the full run

method dtype cases pass fwd pass grad worst fwd err median fwd err
sdpa_math / sdpa_flash_cpu / tiled / tiled_recompute fp64 49 each 100 % 100 % ≤ 3.7e-15 ~3–5e-16
all five exact methods fp32 57 each 100 % 100 % ≤ 6.5e-5 (magnitude 30) ~2.5–3e-7
the four fp32-accumulating methods bf16 53 each 100 % 100 % ≤ 4.0e-3 ~2.1e-3
naive (everything in bf16) bf16 53 73.6 % 94.3 % 0.377 5.7e-3

Two more facts from the same run:

  • Unstable softmax demo (fp32, softmax without subtracting the max): 0 % NaN at max logit 3.4 and 83.8, 17.9 % NaN at max logit 335, 40.3 % at 1340. The stable version's error stayed below 2e-7.
  • The exact methods' fp32 output error stayed flat (about 6e-7 to 2e-6) from L = 128 to 2048 in the scaling run; it did not grow with length.

Key points to remember

  • Compare with tolerances: correct implementations differ in the last bits.
  • The reference is fp64 naive on the same rounded inputs.
  • The metric is max|err| / max|ref|, and relative errors use an explicit floor.
  • fp64 1e-12, fp32 2e-5 (or 4·u·max|S|), bf16 relative to a mixed-precision baseline.
  • Investigation 1: a baseline that is itself bad (naive-in-bf16, error up to 38 %) makes tolerances meaningless.
  • Investigation 2: when a check fails, test a hypothesis about the cause. Here the fp32 logit-rounding floor was shared by every implementation.
  • All fp32-accumulating exact methods passed every check. Naive-in-bf16 failed 14 of 53.

Chapter 12 — The complexity model: theory you can test

What you will learn: how the project turns big-O statements into concrete numbers for each method and configuration; why those numbers are always labeled "theory"; how the theory was checked against counters built into the algorithms; and how the memory guard uses it.

12.1 Purpose

The brief insisted that theory and measurement must stay distinguishable. The project therefore has one module that produces only theoretical estimates, and every estimate it produces is stored under a name beginning with theory_. A measured value never carries that prefix, and a theoretical value never appears without it.

In the code: src/attention_lab/complexity/theory.py, function theoretical_cost(method, shape, params).

12.2 What it computes

For a Shape(B, H, L, d, dtype, causal) and a method's parameters, it returns (among others):

  • score_entries: how many query–key logits the implementation actually evaluates, including masked-but-computed entries (local window wastes about half; padded block slots also count);
  • matmul_flops: 2 × 2 × entries × d for softmax methods (QKᵀ plus PV);
  • elementwise_ops: rough counts of exp, max, divide (reported separately, because they cost very differently from matmul FLOPs on a CPU);
  • aux_fwd_bytes: peak intermediate storage of one inference forward, excluding inputs and outputs;
  • fwd_alloc_bytes = aux_fwd_bytes + the output tensor, comparable with the measured tensor peak;
  • saved_for_bwd_bytes: what autograd keeps between forward and backward;
  • asymptotic_time, asymptotic_aux_memory: the big-O strings.

Method-specific details:

  • tiled: counts tiles exactly, loop by loop, including ragged final tiles and causal tile skipping. Autograd-tiled saves all tiles; recompute saves only lse.
  • local_window: ⌈L/C⌉ · C · (C + w_l + w_r) scores, and band_pairs (the useful ones) counted exactly.
  • block_sparse: builds the actual layout with make_layout, then counts rows × b × K_max × b plus dense global rows, the layout density and the number of active blocks.
  • linear_elu: zero scores for non-causal; for causal, C × C per chunk plus the d × d states.

12.3 Checking theory against the code

A model is only useful if it is right, so the algorithms can report what they actually did. They accept an optional stats={} dictionary and fill in counters as they run (score_entries, tiles, band_entries, active_blocks, k_max).

Scientific tests (tests/scientific/test_complexity_and_measurement.py) then assert exact equality between the theory and the counters:

Test Checks
test_tiled_score_entries_theory_equals_instrumented 8 cases incl. ragged tiles (L = 70 with 16 × 24 tiles; L = 100 with 32 × 7) and causal
test_local_window_entries_theory_equals_instrumented_and_scale_linearly entries and band pairs; 4× longer input ≤ 4.4× entries
test_block_sparse_entries_theory_equals_instrumented entries and active blocks, incl. ragged L = 130 causal
test_naive_entries_are_quadratic doubling L quadruples entries
test_linear_noncausal_has_no_quadratic_term 0 score entries; doubling L doubles FLOPs

What actually happened: the first version of the tiled formula counted tiles × q_tile × kv_tile, which overcounts when the last tile is ragged. It was rewritten to loop over the real tile boundaries so that it equals the counter exactly. Separately, local_window's band_entries statistic was first computed by building a dense L × L band mask, which is O(L²) work inside a supposedly O(L) method. It was replaced by an O(L) formula (band_entry_count) before any benchmark used it.

12.4 Checking theory against measured memory

Chapter 14 compares theory_fwd_alloc_bytes with the measured tensor peak. For naive attention the model predicted 0.875, 3.25, 12.5, 49.0 and 194 MiB at L = 128, 256, 512, 1024 and 2048. The measurements were 0.88, 3.26, 12.52, 49.05 and 194.09 MiB. For methods whose internals are a black box (the fused kernel's per-thread scratch), the model can only give a lower bound, and it says so.

12.5 Use in the memory guard

Before running any configuration, the benchmark runner asks the model for an estimated_peak_bytes for each mode (forward, forward+backward) and refuses modes that would exceed min(50 % of currently available RAM, max_mem_gb). The estimate deliberately overcounts (backward is assumed to need another set of L² temporaries). Refused configurations are recorded with the reason, never silently dropped (Chapter 13).

Key points to remember

  • theory_* fields are estimates, always labeled; measured fields never carry that prefix.
  • The model counts the scores each implementation actually computes, including masked waste and padding.
  • Algorithms expose stats= counters; tests assert theory == counters exactly.
  • The naive memory model matched measurement to within 0.1 MiB.
  • The memory guard uses the model to refuse (and record) configurations that could exhaust RAM.

Chapter 13 — The benchmarking system: measuring time and memory honestly

What you will learn: how one benchmark configuration is run, step by step; how timing is done and summarized; the three memory instruments and what each one really measures (and how the main one was validated); the memory guard; isolated worker processes; the sweep scheduler; and the story of the shared machine, which led to the background-load monitor, CPU-time measurements and single-threaded runs.

13.1 One configuration, step by step

In the code: src/attention_lab/benchmarking/runner.py, run_one(BenchConfig).

A configuration is: method + parameters + B, H, L, d + dtype + causal + threads + warm-up/repeats + seed. The runner executes, in this order (chosen so that the instruments do not contaminate each other):

  1. Theory and environment are recorded (CPU, cores, RAM, OS, Python/torch/numpy versions, thread settings).
  2. Memory guard (per mode): modes whose estimate exceeds the budget are skipped and recorded.
  3. Inputs q, k, v, dout ~ N(0, 1) from a seeded generator.
  4. Timing of each mode, wrapped in the background-load monitor:
    • fwd: forward under torch.inference_mode();
    • fwd_bwd: forward with gradient-requiring inputs, then out.backward(dout).
  5. In isolated mode, the OS peak working set is read after each mode.
  6. Tensor peak of each mode, from a separate untimed call under the profiler.
  7. Error against the fp64 naive reference. This runs last, because the reference is the most memory-hungry step.

The result is one JSON record with every number and every setting.

13.2 Timing

In the code: src/attention_lab/benchmarking/timing.py, time_callable.

  • The first call is timed separately (first_call_s), because it includes one-off costs such as allocator growth and oneDNN setup.
  • warmup untimed calls follow, then repeats timed calls with time.perf_counter_ns(), a monotonic, high-resolution clock.
  • Python's garbage collector is paused during the timed loop.
  • The summary reports the median (the headline number), q1, q3, IQR, MAD, min, max, mean and coefficient of variation, plus every raw sample. The minimum is never reported alone, because it describes the luckiest run rather than typical behaviour.
  • A time budget (max_seconds_per_mode) stops repetition early for slow configurations, and the actual number of repeats done is recorded.
  • Process CPU time per call is recorded too (explained in §13.7).

No test ever asserts a timing threshold. A test that fails because the machine is busy would teach nothing. Correctness and performance are kept separate.

13.3 Three memory instruments

Instrument What it measures What it misses
Tensor peak (memory.tensor_peak_bytes) peak bytes allocated through PyTorch's CPU allocator during one call, reconstructed from profiler [memory] events memory existing before the call (inputs); scratch memory allocated inside MKL/oneDNN/OpenMP outside PyTorch's allocator; Python objects
Process peak Δ (memory.ProcessPeak) Windows' peak working set of the whole process minus its size before the first call it is a lifetime high-water mark, so it needs a fresh process per configuration and the fwd+bwd value is really max(fwd, fwd+bwd); it includes allocator caches; page granularity
Theory (complexity/theory.py) analytical estimate everything not modeled; never reported as measured

How the tensor peak works. The profiler with profile_memory=True records an event every time PyTorch's CPU allocator hands out memory (+bytes) or takes it back (−bytes), with a timestamp. Sorting these events by time and keeping a running sum gives the memory in use at each moment. Its maximum is the peak.

How it was validated. Before any result relied on it, it was tested on a known pattern: allocate 10 MiB, allocate 5 MiB, free the 10 MiB, allocate 3 MiB, free everything. The true peak is 15 MiB (10 + 5), and the instrument reported exactly 15.0 MiB, with a net of 0. Computing one 16 MiB score matrix from 1 MiB of inputs reported 17.0 MiB. Both are now tests (test_tensor_peak_bytes_exact_on_known_allocation_pattern, test_tensor_peak_sees_materialized_scores_and_tiling_reduces_it).

13.4 The memory guard

Before each mode, the runner compares the theoretical estimate with budget = min(mem_fraction × available RAM, max_mem_gb) (defaults 50 % and a few GB). If forward fits but forward+backward does not, it runs forward only and records status = "partial" with modes_skipped_memory. If nothing fits, it records status = "skipped_memory" with the estimate and budget in the reason.

What actually happened: the first guard decided for the whole configuration using the forward+backward estimate. That would have skipped useful forward measurements at large L, so it was changed to decide per mode. Then the scheduler was briefly made to stop growing a series after a "partial" result. That was wrong, because forward-only may still fit at the next length, so it was reverted: a series stops only after a full skipped_memory. The guard did its job repeatedly. For example, at L = 4096 the naive and math methods (about 0.8 GB for forward alone) were skipped when only 0.6–0.8 GB was budgeted, and the free RAM varied from run to run because of other programs.

13.5 Isolated workers

The OS peak working set can only be reset by starting a new process, so the runner can execute a configuration in a fresh Python process (run_isolated → python -m attention_lab.benchmarking.worker, config in on stdin, JSON record out on stdout). The parent sets OMP_NUM_THREADS and MKL_NUM_THREADS before torch is imported in the child, which controls threads more faithfully than set_num_threads alone. Isolation also protects the main process if a configuration runs out of memory.

The cost is that starting Python and importing torch took about 5 s per worker on this machine.

What actually happened: each worker initially also spent 1–2 s asking PowerShell for the CPU name. The parent now passes the name through an environment variable (ATTENTION_LAB_CPU_NAME).

13.6 The scheduler

In the code: src/attention_lab/benchmarking/scheduler.py; specs in experiments/configs/*.yaml.

A YAML spec lists methods (with params), a grid (B, H, L, d, dtype, causal, threads), repeats, budgets and a hypothesis sentence. The scheduler:

  • expands the grid and sorts by L, so every method is measured small before anything large runs;
  • runs configurations one at a time (in-process or isolated);
  • appends each result to results.jsonl immediately, so an interrupted sweep keeps everything measured so far;
  • stops growing a series (same method/shape, larger L) after a memory skip, an error, a timeout, or a median time above stop_if_slower_than_s, recording later configurations as skipped_after_budget with the reason;
  • optionally waits, for a bounded time, for the machine to go quiet before each configuration (wait_for_quiet).

13.7 The shared-machine story

What actually happened. The first full exact-scaling sweep ran with 4 threads in isolated workers. Its numbers looked wrong. At L = 512, tiled and tiled_recompute, whose forward passes run identical code, measured 13.1 ms and 34.7 ms. Causal tiled (half the work) was slower than non-causal tiled. A quick check showed all 12 logical CPUs at 100 %, while the benchmark used only 4 threads.

Listing the Python processes showed why: workloads from other projects were running at the same time (three training scripts, another Transformer experiment, a chess-engine server with its engine processes, and a test run). They were not ours, so they were not touched. But they made fine-grained timing unreliable: a 4-thread OpenMP computation competing with up to 11 busy logical CPUs is slowed by different amounts for different methods.

The response, in steps:

  1. Measure the load. benchmarking/load.py adds a LoadMonitor: a background thread samples system CPU use and this process's CPU use every 0.2 s during each timed region, and records other_load_cores (how many logical CPUs other processes kept busy). Records with more than 1 other busy core are flagged contended. Bug found while testing it: short timed regions finished before the first sample, giving no data. Fixed by priming the counters on entry and always taking a final sample on exit.
  2. Record CPU time. Process CPU time per call excludes time spent waiting for a core. Bug found: on Windows, time.process_time ticks in about 15.6 ms steps, so per-call samples of fast calls read 0.0. Fixed by measuring CPU time over the whole timed loop and dividing by the number of calls.
  3. Wait for quiet, within limits. wait_for_quiet waits up to a timeout for the load to drop. The load stayed high for hours, so the timeout was reduced from 60 s to 10 s per configuration; the load is recorded either way.
  4. Run the definitive timing sweeps single-threaded. With one thread, no OpenMP barrier can stall on a descheduled sibling thread, so contention degrades every method more evenly. The check that this worked: CPU time per call matched wall time within a few percent (for example 509 ms CPU vs 516 ms wall), and the fitted exponents became physically sensible (1.92–2.03, instead of up to 3.0 in the contaminated run).
  5. Never mix contended and clean claims. The first sweep's memory data is used (memory is not affected by CPU contention). Its timing data is reported as contaminated and not used as evidence.

How noisy is the machine? The same naive forward at L = 2048 on one thread measured 392 ms in one sweep and 784 ms in another an hour later. The book therefore compares methods only within a sweep (measured close together in time), and states background load next to every timing table.

13.8 What a GPU benchmark would need

None of this is GPU-specific, and adding a GPU would mean: synchronizing the device before and after each timed call (GPU work is asynchronous), measuring peak memory with torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated after resetting it, warming up kernel autotuning, and recording the GPU model and driver. CPU and GPU numbers must never share a plot without labels. The algorithms themselves need no changes.

Key points to remember

  • Order of measurement: guard → inputs → timing (+ load) → process peak → tensor peak → error.
  • Median + IQR, warm-up, monotonic clock, GC paused, raw samples kept, and no timing assertions in tests.
  • Three memory instruments with different scopes. The tensor peak was validated byte-exactly (15.0 MiB on a 15 MiB pattern).
  • The guard decides per mode and records every skip.
  • Isolated workers give clean process-peak numbers and set threads before torch loads (about 5 s overhead each).
  • The machine was shared. The load was measured, CPU time recorded, definitive sweeps run on 1 thread, and contaminated timings discarded.

Chapter 14 — Results I: the exact methods (correctness, memory, time)

What you will learn: what the experiments showed about the five exact implementations: that they agree numerically; how their memory scales (measured); how their time scales (measured on one thread); and how to read these results without over-reading them.

Conditions for everything in this chapter: B = 1, H = 4, d = 64, fp32, non-causal unless stated. Runs: 20261011-191952_scaling_exact (memory, isolated workers, 4 threads, timing contaminated and not used) and 20261011-210946_scaling_exact_timing (timing, 1 thread, in-process; background load 4.5–10.6 other logical CPUs). Figures are in experiments/reports/<run>/.

14.1 They compute the same function

From Chapter 11: all exact methods agree with the fp64 reference to about 10⁻¹⁵ in fp64 and pass every fp32 check (forward and gradients) across 57 cases each. In the scaling run, the fp32 output error against fp64 stayed between 6 × 10⁻⁷ and 2 × 10⁻⁶ from L = 128 to 2048. It does not grow with length.

14.2 Memory: measured peak tensor allocation per call

L naive fwd sdpa_math fwd flash fwd tiled fwd naive fwd+bwd flash fwd+bwd tiled (autograd) fwd+bwd tiled_recompute fwd+bwd
128 0.88 0.69 0.22 1.13 1.75 0.75 1.13 2.01
512 12.5 9.5 1.07 1.78 25.0 3.51 7.03 3.78
1024 49.0 37.0 3.27 2.54 98.0 9.02 22.0 5.81
2048 194.1 146.0 4.29 4.57 388.0 14.0 76.4 9.88
4096 skipped skipped 6.32 8.63 skipped 24.1 skipped 18.0

(MiB. "skipped" = refused by the memory guard at the time.)

Fitted exponents of memory vs L (L ≥ 512): naive 1.98 / 1.98 (fwd / fwd+bwd); sdpa_math 1.97; flash 0.81 / 0.90; tiled (autograd) 0.77 / 1.72; tiled_recompute 0.84 / 0.75.

What this shows:

  1. Materializing methods are quadratic in memory, exactly as predicted. The theory said 0.875 / 12.5 / 49.0 / 194 MiB for naive; the measurements were 0.88 / 12.5 / 49.0 / 194.1.
  2. Tiling and fusion make forward memory almost linear: 4.3–4.6 MiB at L = 2048, against 194 MiB for naive, a 42–45× reduction.
  3. Autograd through the tile loop brings quadratic memory back for training (exponent 1.72, 76 MiB at 2048).
  4. The recompute backward keeps training memory linear (0.75; 9.9 MiB at 2048, 39× less than naive).
  5. At the process level (OS peak working set, isolated workers), naive needed 446 MiB more than its starting size at L = 2048 for fwd+bwd, against 57 MiB for the flash kernel. About 35–40 MiB of that is fixed overhead, visible even at L = 128.

Figure 14.1 (below) shows all methods on one log-log plot against dashed L and L² guides. Naive and math track the L² line; flash and recompute track the L line; autograd-tiled bends toward L² in fwd+bwd.

Figure 14.1 — Measured peak tensor memory per call vs L, all exact methods on shared log-log axes (run 20261011-191952_scaling_exact). Dashed grey lines are theory slopes ∝ L and ∝ L².

14.3 Time: measured on one thread

Median milliseconds per call:

L naive fwd sdpa_math fwd flash fwd tiled fwd recompute fwd naive fwd+bwd math fwd+bwd flash fwd+bwd tiled fwd+bwd recompute fwd+bwd
256 4.1 5.3 2.6 5.1 5.5 16.0 10.5 10.7 19.6 20.1
512 28.1 23.6 8.4 21.8 23.3 82.4 54.7 36.4 75.1 68.7
1024 105.5 86.5 31.5 73.4 87.7 304.4 210.0 135.9 353.1 268.7
2048 392.4 355.6 146.7 313.0 345.0 1411.2 803.7 503.9 1847.0 979.9
4096 1540.4 1512.9 515.6 1445.4 1600.3 (guard) (guard) 2017.0 14489.5 4637.2

Fitted exponents of time vs L (wall clock / CPU time): every exact method's forward is 1.92–2.03 (CPU 1.97–2.10). Forward+backward is 1.91–2.05 for all of them except autograd-tiled at 2.52.

What this shows:

  1. Every exact method is quadratic in time, including the memory-efficient ones. Tiling moves the scores into small tiles; it does not reduce how many scores there are.
  2. The fused CPU kernel is the fastest exact method at every length: about 3× faster than naive in forward (516 vs 1,540 ms at L = 4096) and 2.8× in fwd+bwd at 2048. Same arithmetic, so the gain is fusion (no L² tensor ever written to RAM) and no Python dispatch per step.
  3. On one thread, our Python tiled forward was not slower than naive. It was 6–30 % faster at L ≥ 512 (313 vs 392 ms at 2048). Its per-tile dispatch overhead is offset by avoiding three L² tables that overflow the 16 MB L3 cache. This depends on threads: in the saved 4-thread runs, tiled was much slower than naive (6.3 vs 0.7 ms at L = 256 in the smoke run; 13.1 vs 5.2 ms at 512 in the contended run), and Chapter 15's thread experiment explains why.
  4. Storing costs more than recomputing. tiled_recompute does 25 % more backward arithmetic than autograd-tiled, yet fwd+bwd took 980 ms vs 1,847 ms at 2048, and 4.6 s vs 14.5 s at 4096. Autograd-tiled's super-quadratic exponent (2.52) indicates growing memory-system cost from keeping every tile alive.
  5. Fusion still wins over the best Python version: flash fwd+bwd 504 ms vs recompute 980 ms at 2048. The algorithm is the same; the execution is not.

Figure 14.2 — Measured median time per call vs L on one thread (run 20261011-210946_scaling_exact_timing), with IQR bars. Every exact method runs parallel to the L² guide.

14.4 How not to read these results

  • They are CPU results. A GPU has different cache sizes, bandwidth, launch costs and bf16 support, and the ratios would differ.
  • The absolute times include background load (flagged contended). Ratios measured in the same sweep, close together in time, are more trustworthy than absolute numbers.
  • "Tiled ≈ naive on one thread" is a statement about this Python implementation, this tile size (128) and one thread, not about tiling in general.

Key points to remember

  • All exact methods agree numerically (≈ 1e-15 fp64, ≈ 1e-6 fp32).
  • Memory: naive/math ∝ L² (194 MiB at 2048); flash/tiled ∝ L (≈ 4.5 MiB); training: autograd-tiled ∝ L^1.72, recompute ∝ L^0.75.
  • Time: everything exact ∝ L² (1.9–2.1).
  • Fused kernel ≈ 3× faster than naive; recompute faster than storing (980 vs 1,847 ms).
  • Single-thread Python tiled ≈ naive or better; multi-thread it is much worse (Chapter 15).

Chapter 15 — Results II: approximate methods, tile sizes, threads, shapes and number formats

What you will learn: when the approximate methods actually beat the best exact kernel, and when they do not; the surprising memory result; how tile size shapes the Python tiled kernel's speed and memory; how each method responds to more threads; and how head dimension, batch and bf16 affect time.

15.1 Approximate methods vs the fused exact kernel (E2)

Run: 20261011-212017_scaling_approx: isolated workers, 1 thread, B = 1, H = 4, d = 64, fp32. local_window w = 64; block_sparse b = 64 (±1 local, global 0, 1 random); linear_elu chunk 64. 55 of 56 configurations measured. The fused kernel at L = 16,384 non-causal was skipped by the time budget, because its fwd+bwd at 8,192 took 8.4 s. Background load was mostly 6–11 other logical CPUs, so single points are noisy and trends are reliable.

Median forward time (ms), non-causal / causal:

256 2.7 / 2.6 9.7 / 6.9 8.2 / 10.7 2.0 / 5.3
1,024 32.7 / 27.5 37.4 / 21.8 57.0 / 44.4 8.4 / 19.7
2,048 131.2 / 82.5 86.4 / 50.7 143.9 / 97.1 16.6 / 48.6

Fitted time exponents: local_window 0.82–1.02, block_sparse 0.89–0.97, linear_elu 0.90–0.97 (linear in L); flash 1.73–1.99 (quadratic).

Figure 15.1 — Measured runtime vs L for the approximate methods and the fused exact kernel (run 20261011-212017_scaling_approx).

Findings.

  1. Linear in theory, linear in measurement: every approximate method's time grows about ∝ L.
  2. But they only win beyond a crossover. In non-causal forward, linear_elu is faster at every measured length, local_window from about 2,048 tokens, and block_sparse is roughly even at 2,048 and clearly faster from 4,096. Below about 1,024 tokens, local_window and block_sparse are 1.1–3.6× slower than the fused exact kernel, even though they evaluate far fewer scores: padding, unfold copies, gathering and masked waste cost more than they save at short lengths.
  3. At long lengths the gap is large: at L = 8,192 non-causal, flash takes 2.4 s, local_window 0.39 s (6.2×) and linear_elu 0.06 s (41×).
  4. Causal attention narrows the gap, because the fused kernel skips tiles above the diagonal: its causal forward is 1.2× faster than its non-causal one at L = 1,024, rising to 2.4× at 8,192.

15.2 The memory surprise

Measured tensor peak per forward call (MiB), non-causal:

L flash (exact) local_window block_sparse linear_elu naive (Chapter 14)
1,024 1.6 19.0 29.4 4.1 49.0
4,096 4.6 74.5 122.6 16.2 (guard)
16,384 — 296.3 496.1 64.6 —

Figure 15.2 — Measured peak tensor memory, approximate methods vs the fused exact kernel.

"Approximate attention saves memory" is false relative to a fused exact kernel. All three approximate methods allocate more than sdpa_flash_cpu at every length: 16× (local) and 27× (block sparse) more at 4,096 tokens. They materialize O(L·window) score tables or gathered key blocks, while the fused kernel streams small tiles and allocates little beyond its output. The approximate methods save memory only relative to materializing exact methods: at L = 1,024, local_window needs 19 MiB against naive's 49 MiB, and the gap widens with L. The theory model predicted this (Chapter 10 §10.5). The measurement confirms it.

This is Principle B of the project in its purest form: memory efficiency, computational efficiency and asymptotic class are three different things.

Deviation from full softmax (relative Frobenius norm, random inputs, non-causal): local_window grows from 1.15 to 3.85 between L = 256 and 2,048, block_sparse from 0 (its layout is dense at L = 256) to 2.32, and linear_elu stays about 0.75–0.79. On random inputs attention is diffuse, so dropping most keys changes outputs by more than their own size. This number describes how much the function changes. Quality is measured by the probes and tasks.

15.3 Tile size in the Python tiled kernels (E3)

Run: 20261011-215718_tile_sizes (L = 2,048, 1 thread). Heavily contended (about 11 other logical CPUs for every config), so compare only within this run. (naive measured 784 ms here, against 392 ms in Chapter 14.)

implementation tile Python tile iterations fwd (ms) fwd tensor peak (MiB) fwd+bwd (ms) fwd+bwd peak (MiB)
tiled (autograd) 32 4,096 1,941 4.1 41,418 79.0
tiled (autograd) 64 1,024 704 4.3 4,693 77.1
tiled (autograd) 128 256 528 4.6 4,177 76.4
tiled (autograd) 256 64 639 5.6 2,190 75.8
tiled (autograd) 512 16 899 14.6 1,391 79.1
tiled_recompute 32 4,096 1,478 4.1 4,523 8.3
tiled_recompute 128 256 466 4.6 1,362 9.9
tiled_recompute 512 16 442 14.6 1,273 33.1
naive — — 784 194.1 2,258 388.0
sdpa_flash_cpu — — 152 2.6 773 11.0
  1. Forward time is U-shaped in tile size, with the minimum at 128. Tiny tiles drown in Python and dispatcher overhead (4,096 iterations at tile 32, 3.7× slower than tile 128). Big tiles slow down again: a 512 × 512 tile for 4 heads is 4 MiB, against the 512 KB per-core L2 cache, while tile 128 is 256 KiB. The cache explanation fits but was not measured with hardware counters.
  2. Forward memory stays flat until the tile² term dominates (4.1 → 4.6 → 14.6 MiB).
  3. Tile size cannot fix autograd's training memory: 76–79 MiB at every tile size. Small tiles are disastrous for autograd's backward time (41 s at tile 32), because it records and replays about 10 graph nodes per tile.
  4. The recompute backward stays at 8–10 MiB for tiles ≤ 128 and is 1.1–9.2× faster than autograd at equal tile size.
  5. Even at its best tile, Python tiling is 3.1–3.5× slower than the fused kernel.

15.4 Threads (E4)

Run: 20261011-221221_threads (L = 2,048, isolated workers, threads 1/2/4/6). Background load about 9–11 other logical CPUs for naive/flash/tiled, about 3–9 for linear/local. Indicative.

method 1 thread (ms) 2 4 6 speed-up at 2 / 4 / 6
sdpa_flash_cpu 124.3 85.9 42.7 35.1 1.45 / 2.91 / 3.54
naive 402.9 319.2 234.3 230.0 1.26 / 1.72 / 1.75
linear_elu 7.8 4.5 4.0 3.5 1.74 / 1.95 / 2.23
local_window 35.6 29.1 23.4 42.0 1.22 / 1.52 / 0.85
